hook: Hundreds of millions of photos arrive every day. Why can't a database or a big server disk hold them?
title: Write once, read for days, then never: meet object storage
body:
Your app has 1 billion users uploading hundreds of millions of photos and videos a day. Each file is large, written once, read heavily for a few days, then almost never touched. Nobody edits a photo in place; a filter saves a new file.

A database is the wrong home. A disk on one server is too small, dies with the server, and only one machine can read it. You need **object storage**: trillions of immutable blobs, never lost, served over HTTP, cheap per byte.
takeaway: The access pattern picks the storage system, not the other way round.
deeper:
**Write-once removes the hard part:** A photo app never edits a file in place, so the store never has to support in-place updates. That single absence simplifies everything downstream.

**Cold bytes set the price:** Most photos are read for days and then sit idle for years. For that long tail, cost per stored byte matters far more than speed. Later designs, from erasure coding to age-based tiers, all chase that cost.

**Three tests, three failures:** Capacity is bounded by one machine. Durability is bounded by one machine's lifetime. Access is bounded by one machine's network card. Object storage removes all three bounds: capacity spread over a fleet, redundancy across failures, and plain HTTP so any client anywhere can fetch a blob.

**The catch:** The same design that makes blobs cheap makes small edits impossible. That is fine for photos and fatal for a database's data files.

quiz.q: A team plans to store user-uploaded videos on a large RAID array attached to their main app server. Name three ways this breaks at a billion users.
quiz.a: Capacity is capped by one machine, the videos die with that server, and only that machine can serve them. Object storage spreads capacity, redundancy and HTTP access across a fleet.

mcq.q: Which property of photo uploads makes object storage's no-edit rule harmless?
options: Files are written once and never edited in place
Files are small enough to fit in a database row
Files are read most heavily years after upload
Files are always read by the server that wrote them
mcq.why: Applying a filter saves a new file, so the store never needs to support in-place updates to existing objects.

hook: In S3, a key like photos/cat.jpg carries no region, no permissions, no settings. So where do they live?
title: Bucket + key = one object. That's the whole model.
body:
An **object** is a blob of bytes plus a little metadata: content type, size, checksum and user-defined key-value tags. It lives in a **bucket**, a named container that carries the settings: region, access policy, versioning, lifecycle rules, encryption.

Inside the bucket, the object's **key** is just a string, like `photos/2026/09/26/user-123/img-9f2c.jpg`. The key carries no settings at all. Bucket plus key gives you exactly one object, and you read or replace it whole.
takeaway: Policy lives on the bucket; the key is only a name.
deeper:
**Buckets are governance units:** Because region, access, versioning, lifecycle and encryption are bucket settings, teams often split data into separate buckets because it needs different retention or access rules, not because of size.

**Keys are performance design:** The key's structure is up to you, and it matters. S3 partitions its index by key range, so the shape of your keys decides how load spreads across partitions. A key that looks like a harmless name can funnel all your traffic into one partition.

**Metadata is small on purpose:** It describes the blob; it does not replace a database. You cannot list objects by tag, only by key prefix. Anything you will want to search by later, such as the owning user or a content label, belongs in a separate index that maps attributes to keys.

**The catch:** Moving an object to a bucket with different rules means copying it to a new bucket and key.

quiz.q: A teammate wants some photos stored in the EU and some in the US, all in one bucket, chosen per object. Why won't that work in S3's model?
quiz.a: Region is a bucket setting, not a per-object setting. Data that must live in different regions needs different buckets.

mcq.q: Which setting is attached to an S3 bucket rather than to each object?
options: The region where the data lives
The object's content type
The object's checksum
User-defined key-value tags
mcq.why: Region, access policy, versioning, lifecycle and encryption are bucket settings. Content type, checksum and tags are per-object metadata.

hook: Renaming one 'folder' of photos in S3 can take a million operations. Why can't it just change one name?
title: S3 folders don't exist. The slashes are just characters.
body:
In an S3 general purpose bucket, `photos/2026/` looks like a folder. It isn't. The **namespace is flat**: each key is one opaque string, and the slashes are just characters in it.

When a console shows folders, it runs a list request with a **prefix** (`photos/2026/`) and a delimiter (`/`), then groups the results. There is no directory object to rename, lock or delete. So renaming a folder means copying every object to a new key and deleting the old one.
takeaway: No directories means no cheap renames: a folder rename is N copies plus N deletes.
deeper:
**Why flat wins at scale:** A real filesystem must keep directory entries, keep parents and children consistent, and support atomic subtree renames. Each is a coordination problem that gets much harder across over 280 trillion objects on many machines. A flat key space turns the index into a sorted map from key to location, which splits cleanly by key range.

**Where it bites:** A rename of N objects is N copies plus N deletes. It is slow, it costs requests, and it is not atomic: a reader mid-rename can see some objects under the old prefix and some under the new. Tools that make S3 look like a filesystem hide this until a big rename runs for hours.

**The exception:** S3 Express One Zone uses directory buckets, which do have a real hierarchical namespace, and their list results come back unsorted. The flat model applies to general purpose buckets.

quiz.q: A job renames `raw/` to `archive/` across 5 million objects and crashes halfway. What does a reader listing both prefixes see, and why?
quiz.a: Some objects under `raw/`, some under `archive/`, possibly both copies of a few. A folder rename is per-object copy then delete, with no atomic directory operation to roll back.

mcq.q: How does the S3 console display 'folders' in a general purpose bucket?
options: A list request with a prefix and / delimiter, grouped
Directory objects stored alongside the data objects
A separate folder index maintained per bucket
A hierarchy table kept in the bucket's settings
mcq.why: The namespace is flat. The console lists with a prefix and delimiter and groups the results, so no directory object exists.

predict.q: Renaming an S3 'folder' holding 1 million objects costs roughly how many operations?
options: About 2 million: a copy and a delete per object
One: a single metadata rename
About 1,000: one per listing page

hook: Two clients upload the same key at the same instant. Can a reader ever get half of each file?
title: You can't change byte 500. That's what makes S3 safe.
body:
On a shared file, two processes writing different offsets at once can leave a file that belongs to neither. Object storage refuses to play. An object is **immutable**: you cannot change byte 500 of it. You can only replace the whole object with a new `PUT`, or delete it.

So two writers can never interleave bytes inside one object. If two clients upload the same key, each upload is complete, and the **last complete PUT wins**. Readers see one whole version, never a mix.
takeaway: Refuse partial writes and a whole class of concurrency bugs disappears.
deeper:
**No locks needed:** Preventing interleaved writes on a normal file takes locks, leases or careful protocols, all hard to run across a global fleet. With whole-object replacement as the only unit of change, the system only has to decide which complete version is current.

**The catch:** Last-writer-wins can silently throw work away. A slow upload that started first can finish last and replace a newer one. Nothing errors; the newer data is simply no longer the current version.

**Two fixes on top:** Versioning keeps every PUT as its own version, so the overwritten one is still recoverable. Conditional writes, added to S3 in 2024, let a client say 'only create if absent' (`If-None-Match: *`) or 'only replace if unchanged' (`If-Match` with an ETag), which gives compare-and-swap on the immutable model.

**Wrong fit:** Workloads that edit small parts of big files, like database data files, belong on block storage.

quiz.q: Two phones upload edited versions of `avatar.jpg`. Phone A starts first but is on slow Wi-Fi and finishes last. With no versioning or conditions, what does the next reader get?
quiz.a: Phone A's upload, complete and intact, because the last complete PUT wins. Phone B's newer edit is silently replaced; versioning or a conditional write would have protected it.

mcq.q: Why can two concurrent PUTs to one S3 key never leave interleaved bytes?
options: Objects are replaced whole; partial writes don't exist
S3 locks the key for the duration of each upload
The front end queues writes to a key in arrival order
Each PUT is written to a separate Availability Zone
mcq.why: An object is immutable. The only change is a complete new PUT, so readers always get one whole version, from the last complete PUT.

hook: Cache invalidation is famously hard. Why do object stores barely have to think about it?
title: An object never changes, so a copy is never 'a bit stale'
body:
A cached copy of a mutable file can drift from the source one byte at a time. A cached copy of a given object version cannot: it is either exactly the right version or a different version. **Immutability** gives replication the same gift.

It also makes **erasure coding** cheap. The system cuts an object into pieces and computes parity once, at write time. It never recomputes parity because a small region changed, because no small region ever changes.
takeaway: Compute parity once, never again: immutability makes redundancy cheap.
deeper:
**The small-write penalty, avoided:** If erasure-coded data could be edited in place, every small write would mean reading old data and old parity, computing new parity, and writing both back. Immutable objects skip that forever. Parity is computed exactly once.

**Caching becomes a version question:** Invalidation is hard when a copy can drift bit by bit. When a version can never change, a cache only has to know which version is current. Any copy of that version is byte-for-byte correct.

**Replication ships whole versions:** Copying to another place means sending the complete new version, never a stream of partial patches that must be applied in order.

**The catch:** A database that rewrites small pages inside a multi-gigabyte file would have to rewrite the whole object for every change. That is why database data files go to block storage instead.

quiz.q: A CDN holds version 7 of an object. The origin now has version 8. Is the CDN's copy corrupt, partially stale, or something else?
quiz.a: Neither corrupt nor partially stale. It is a complete, correct copy of version 7; it is simply a different version. Freshness is only a question of which version is current.

mcq.q: Why does immutability make erasure coding cheap for object stores?
options: Parity is computed once at write time and never updated
Immutable objects need fewer parity shards than mutable ones
Parity can be skipped for objects that are rarely read
Immutable objects compress better before encoding
mcq.why: No small region ever changes, so the read-old-data, recompute-parity, write-back cycle for small edits never happens.

hook: You need to relabel a million S3 objects without rewriting a single byte. Which kind of metadata lets you?
title: Tags change freely; user metadata is frozen at upload
body:
Objects carry two kinds of metadata. **System metadata** is set by the service: size, last-modified time, ETag, storage class, encryption state. The **ETag** identifies the content and is often an MD5 for simple uploads. User metadata is small key-value pairs you attach at upload time, and it stays fixed with the object.

Object **tags** are the escape hatch. You can change them later without rewriting the object, and lifecycle and access policies can act on them.
takeaway: Need a label you'll change later? Make it a tag, not metadata.
deeper:
**Why the split exists:** Metadata follows the immutability rule unevenly. User metadata belongs to the object as uploaded, so changing it effectively means writing the object again. Tags are mutable labels stored alongside it, cheap to update.

**Tags as selectors:** A lifecycle rule can move or expire only objects with a given tag, and an access policy can grant or deny by tag. That makes tags a control surface, not just a label.

**Read the ETag carefully:** For simple uploads it is often the MD5 of the content, handy for integrity checks and change detection. Don't assume it is an MD5 for every upload type; treat it as an opaque content identifier. It also powers conditional writes: `If-Match` with an ETag fails if the object changed since you read it.

**The catch:** Neither tags nor metadata are searchable. They describe an object once you know its key.

quiz.q: A compliance team must mark 10 million existing objects so a lifecycle rule moves only those to an archive class. User metadata or tags, and why?
quiz.a: Tags. They can be changed later without rewriting the objects, and lifecycle policies can act on them. Changing user metadata would mean rewriting every object.

mcq.q: Which is true of an S3 object's ETag?
options: It identifies the content, often an MD5 for simple uploads
It is a mutable label that lifecycle rules can act on
It is a user-defined value set at upload time
It records the storage class the object was first written to
mcq.why: The ETag is system metadata identifying the content, often the MD5 for simple uploads. Tags are the mutable labels.

hook: Your PM asks for every photo tagged 'cat'. S3 holds all the tags. Why can't it answer?
title: S3 can't find objects by tag. It only lists by key prefix.
body:
It is tempting to treat object metadata as a query engine. You cannot ask S3 for every object where user-tag = cat. **Listing is by key prefix only.** Metadata and tags describe an object once you know its key; they never help you find keys.

Big companies keep a **separate index**, such as a database table or an Iceberg table, that maps business attributes like user, date or label to object keys. The index answers the query; S3 serves the bytes.
takeaway: The object store holds bytes; your index holds meaning.
deeper:
**Why S3 can't do it:** The index layer maps bucket, key and version to where the bytes live, partitioned by key range. It answers 'what is at this key' and 'which keys start with this prefix', because both are range lookups on a sorted map. A tag query would mean reading every object's metadata. At billions of objects, that is a full scan.

**The pattern that works:** Write to the object store and to a queryable index in the same upload pipeline. The database or table keeps attributes and returns keys; you then `GET` the bytes. The same index removes most reasons to list the bucket at all.

**The catch:** Skip this early and the bill arrives later as a backfill. Someone asks for last year's cat photos, and the only option is scanning everything.

quiz.q: An ML team wants every image labelled 'dog' from a 2-billion-object bucket, and labels exist only as object tags. What are their options, and what should they have built on day one?
quiz.a: Only a full scan of every object's tags, since S3 lists by prefix alone. They should have written labels to a separate index mapping attributes to keys at upload.

mcq.q: How do large companies look up S3 objects by business attributes?
options: A separate database or Iceberg table maps attributes to keys
S3's index layer supports secondary indexes on tags
A filtered ListObjectsV2 call that matches tag values
User metadata queries run through the S3 front end
mcq.why: S3 lists only by key prefix. An external index answers attribute queries and returns keys, which you then fetch.

hook: An engineer deletes the wrong prefix in a versioned bucket. How much data is actually gone?
title: In a versioned bucket, DELETE removes nothing
body:
With **versioning** on, every `PUT` to a key creates a new version ID instead of overwriting. A `DELETE` without a version ID removes no data at all. It adds a **delete marker**, which hides the object from normal reads, while older versions stay readable and restorable.

That makes versioning the cheapest protection against a bug or a person that deletes or overwrites data. The cost is storage: old versions are billed until a lifecycle rule expires them.
takeaway: Versioning turns 'deleted' into 'hidden', and hidden can be undone.
deeper:
**Why it matters most:** Most real data loss comes from software and people, not simultaneous disk failures. Erasure coding faithfully stores a wrong instruction; versioning keeps the previous answer. A job that overwrites a million objects with empty files leaves every earlier version intact.

**Recovery is mechanical:** Remove the delete markers, or copy the prior version back on top.

**The billing surprise:** A bucket with frequent overwrites can quietly hold many times its visible size in old versions, all billed. The standard fix is a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after a chosen window, so the safety net lasts days or weeks, not forever.

**The catch:** A `DELETE` that names a specific version ID does permanently remove that version. Who may issue versioned deletes is itself a permission to guard.

quiz.q: A buggy job overwrites 1 million objects with empty files in a versioned bucket. What did it destroy, and how do you recover?
quiz.a: Nothing permanent. Each overwrite created a new version; the prior versions remain. Copy the previous version of each key back on top, then expire the empty ones.

mcq.q: In a versioned S3 bucket, what does a DELETE without a version ID do?
options: Adds a delete marker that hides the object
Permanently removes the newest version only
Permanently removes every version of the key
Moves the object to a cheaper storage class
mcq.why: No data is removed. The delete marker hides the key from normal reads; older versions remain readable and restorable.

hook: Your 20 GB upload dies at 19 GB. With the right API, how much do you have to resend?
title: Never restart a 20 GB upload at 19 GB
body:
One HTTP request for a 20 GB video is fragile: break the connection at 19 GB and you start over. **Multipart upload** fixes it. The client calls `CreateMultipartUpload`, uploads parts in parallel, retries any failed part on its own, then calls `CompleteMultipartUpload` with the part list.

S3 makes the object appear **atomically**. Readers never see a half-built file, and parallel parts raise throughput.
takeaway: Split big uploads so a failure costs one part, not the whole file.
deeper:
**The limits:** Current S3 limits are 1 to 10,000 parts, each 5 MiB to 5 GiB (the last part can be smaller), and a maximum object size of 48.8 TiB. AWS suggests multipart once objects reach about 100 MB.

**Atomic completion:** Until `CompleteMultipartUpload` succeeds, no object exists at that key. A reader gets the whole object or nothing.

**The hidden bill:** Parts from uploads that were never completed or aborted are invisible in normal listings, yet still stored and billed. A fleet of clients that crash mid-upload can build a large invisible bill over months. Add a lifecycle rule with `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` to every bucket.

**Part size is a knob:** Smaller parts mean cheaper retries and more parallelism, but more requests. Do the math: 10,000 parts × 5 GiB is the 48.8 TiB ceiling, so very large objects force large parts.

quiz.q: Your bucket's bill grows every month, but listings show the same total object size. Uploads come from flaky mobile clients. What's the likely cause and fix?
quiz.a: Abandoned multipart uploads: their parts are invisible in listings but still billed. Add a lifecycle rule with AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload to clean them up.

mcq.q: Why must very large multipart uploads use large parts?
options: S3 allows at most 10,000 parts per upload
Parts under 1 GiB are rejected for large objects
Small parts cannot be uploaded in parallel
The last part must be at least half the object
mcq.why: With a 10,000-part cap, object size divided by 10,000 sets the minimum part size; 5 GiB parts reach the 48.8 TiB maximum.

hook: For years, two writers could both believe they created the same S3 file. What one header fixed it?
title: 2024: S3 got compare-and-swap, no lock service needed
body:
For many years S3 had no compare-and-swap, so anything needing 'create if absent' had to bring an external lock service. Since 2024 S3 supports **conditional writes**. A `PUT` with `If-None-Match: *` fails with `412 Precondition Failed` if the key exists. A `PUT` with `If-Match: <etag>` fails if the object changed.

When several conditional writes race on one key, the **first to finish wins** and the rest get 412. Table formats can now commit atomically on S3 itself.
takeaway: One atomic 'create if absent' is enough to build coordination on.
deeper:
**The problem it solved:** A table format committing a new snapshot must ensure two writers cannot both claim the next version. Without an atomic check, both write, and one commit silently overwrites the other. Teams ran external databases or lock services just to referee these commits: more cost, more latency, one more thing to fail.

**How a commit works now:**
1. A writer reads the current table state.
2. It tries to create the next metadata file with `If-None-Match: *`.
3. A 412 means someone else got there first.
4. It retries on top of the new state.

**Optimistic updates too:** `If-Match` lets you read an object, note its ETag, and write back only if nobody changed it in between.

**The catch:** S3-compatible systems vary in whether they support newer APIs like this. Test before you rely on it.

quiz.q: Two Spark jobs try to commit version 42 of a table at the same moment, both using `If-None-Match: *` on the same metadata key. What does each see?
quiz.a: The first to finish succeeds; the other gets 412 Precondition Failed, learns it lost, and retries on top of version 42. Neither overwrites the other.

mcq.q: A PUT with If-None-Match: * targets a key that already exists. What happens?
options: It fails with 412 Precondition Failed
It overwrites the object and returns the old ETag
It creates a new version beside the existing one
It waits until the existing object is deleted
mcq.why: If-None-Match: * means 'only if absent'. An existing key makes the precondition fail with 412.

hook: S3 is one of the largest storage systems ever built, and AWS never published its design. What do we know?
title: S3: 280 trillion objects, 100M requests/sec, no paper
body:
Amazon S3 launched on March 14, 2006 and defined the object storage category. By 2023, Andy Warfield described it as hundreds of microservices storing data on millions of hard drives, holding over 280 trillion objects and serving over 100 million requests per second on average.

AWS has never published a **full design paper** for S3. Everything known about its internals comes from what AWS engineers have said in papers, blog posts and talks.
takeaway: At millions of drives, failure is not an event. It is the weather.
deeper:
**Per-object costs multiply:** At over 280 trillion objects, any per-object metadata overhead becomes enormous. That is why the index is its own distributed system, surrounded by services for placement, repair, auditing, lifecycle, replication and billing.

**Nothing central, ever:** Over 100 million requests per second on average means the front end must be stateless and horizontally scalable. No single component can serve every request without being partitioned.

**Failure is the background condition:** With millions of hard drives, some fail every day. Durability has to come from redundancy plus continuous repair, not from reliable hardware.

**The caveat:** With no full design paper, be careful with claims about S3 internals. Trust what AWS engineers have stated: Warfield, Werner Vogels's blog posts, and the SOSP 2021 ShardStore paper.

quiz.q: A colleague says S3's durability comes mainly from unusually reliable drives. Using S3's scale, explain why that can't be the main answer.
quiz.a: With millions of drives, failures happen daily whatever the model. Durability must come from redundancy plus constant detection and repair, which work even with ordinary failing drives.

mcq.q: By 2023, roughly how many requests per second did S3 serve on average?
options: Over 100 million
Over 1 million
Over 10 billion
Over 280 trillion
mcq.why: Warfield's 2023 figures: over 280 trillion objects and over 100 million requests per second on average, on millions of hard drives.

hook: Every S3 GET, PUT, DELETE and LIST passes through one particular layer. Which one, and why?
title: S3 in three layers: front end, index, storage fleet
body: Conceptually S3 has three layers. The **front end** is a fleet of stateless web servers that terminate HTTPS, authenticate (signature, IAM and bucket policy) and route. The **index** is a sharded key-value system mapping bucket, key and version to where the bytes live; every GET, PUT, DELETE and LIST touches it. The **storage layer** is a huge fleet of hard-drive nodes running ShardStore, holding the actual shards.
takeaway: Split by scaling axis: requests, object count and bytes each get their own layer.
deeper:
**One axis per layer:** The front end scales with request rate and auth work; because it is stateless, adding capacity means adding machines. The index scales with object count and metadata operations. The storage layer scales with bytes and disk I/O.

**Why key design matters:** The index is sharded by key range. A hot key range means a hot index partition, no matter how idle the rest of the fleet is.

**The supporting cast:** Background services run around the three layers. Placement decides where new shards go, repair rebuilds lost ones, auditing verifies stored data, lifecycle moves or expires objects, replication copies across regions, billing meters usage. A witness beside the index tracks the latest write per object for strong consistency.

**A recurring shape:** The same metadata-over-data split shows up in Azure, Colossus and Meta's systems.

quiz.q: S3's storage fleet is healthy and mostly idle, yet one customer sees throttled writes. Which layer is the likely bottleneck, and what about their keys would you check?
quiz.a: The index layer, which is sharded by key range. If their keys cluster in one range, one index partition is hot regardless of idle storage nodes.

mcq.q: Which S3 layer maps (bucket, key, version) to where the bytes live?
options: The index layer
The front end
The storage layer
The witness
mcq.why: The index is a sharded key-value system from (bucket, key, version) to location plus system metadata; every request touches it.

hook: A crash hits halfway through a PUT. Could a reader ever find an object with missing bytes?
title: Data first, index last: the index entry is the commit
body:
An S3 `PUT` flows roughly like this: the front end authenticates, the data is cut into shards and written to storage nodes across Availability Zones, and only after the data is durable is the index entry written.

That order is everything. If the index pointed to data not yet safe, a crash could expose a live object with missing bytes. Writing metadata last makes the index entry the **commit point**.
takeaway: The last atomic step of a write decides whether it happened.
deeper:
**Invisible until committed:** Before the index entry exists, the object is invisible to every reader, however many shards are already on disk. After it exists, the data is guaranteed durable, because it was written first.

**Crash in the middle:** A crash between the two steps leaves shards no index entry points to. That is harmless garbage, and background cleanup removes it later.

**Reverse order, silent loss:** Index first, then a crash before the data is durable, publishes an object that cannot be fully read. From the customer's view, the object exists and its data is gone.

**A universal rule:** Multipart upload's atomic completion follows the same idea. Every large object store separates an index layer from an append-only data layer and commits by writing the index entry last.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes writing the index entry first 'so the object shows up faster', then streaming the shards. What failure does this create?
quiz.a: A crash after the index write but before the data is durable exposes a live object with missing bytes. Data-first means a crash only leaves unreferenced garbage.

mcq.q: A crash hits after S3 wrote an object's shards but before its index entry. What is left behind?
options: Unreferenced shards that background cleanup removes
A visible object that returns partial bytes
A delete marker hiding the new object
An index entry pointing at missing shards
mcq.why: Without an index entry the object is invisible. The orphaned shards are garbage, later removed by background cleanup.

predict.q: A PUT must write data shards and an index entry. To survive a crash at any moment, which goes first?
options: Data shards first, index entry last
Index entry first, data shards last
Both at once, in parallel

hook: Crash-safe at every instant, and constantly changing. Why is that combination where storage bugs breed?
title: ShardStore: S3's bottom layer, rewritten in Rust
body:
**ShardStore** is the key-value store running on every S3 storage node, holding the shards of object data. It was a rewrite of S3's bottom-most layer, written in Rust for type safety. The SOSP 2021 paper describes a **log-structured** design that must survive crashes at any moment while the team keeps adding features.

That pairing is where storage engines grow subtle bugs: every new feature adds code paths that must stay correct if power vanishes mid-step.
takeaway: Memory safety is not crash safety. Rust can't prove your recovery logic.
deeper:
**What log-structured costs:** New data is appended rather than written in place, which suits hard drives and immutable shards. But the index over the log, garbage collection of dead data, and crash recovery must all agree on what state is valid. Each path has to be right when power disappears mid-update or mid-compaction.

**What Rust buys, and doesn't:** Rust removes a class of memory-safety and type errors at compile time. It does not prove that crash-recovery logic is correct.

**The real story:** Full formal proofs of a large, fast-changing engine are too expensive. So AWS used lightweight formal methods: an executable reference model, property-based testing against it, and model checking of concurrent code.

**Why change is central:** Any verification method that cannot keep pace with new features eventually stops being used.

quiz.q: A team argues that rewriting their storage engine in Rust means they can skip crash testing. What class of bugs are they still exposed to?
quiz.a: Crash-consistency and concurrency bugs: recovery, log indexing and garbage collection disagreeing about valid state after a crash at the wrong instant. Type safety doesn't prove those correct.

mcq.q: What is ShardStore?
options: The key-value store on every S3 storage node
S3's sharded index of bucket and key locations
The in-memory witness for S3's metadata cache
A Rust library clients use to split uploads
mcq.why: ShardStore is the per-node, log-structured key-value store holding object shards, a Rust rewrite of S3's bottom-most layer.

hook: AWS tests S3's storage engine against a copy 1% its size. How can the tiny one catch bugs in the big one?
title: A model 1% the size checks the real engine
body:
Full proofs of a large, fast-changing storage engine cost too much. So the ShardStore team wrote an **executable reference model** in Rust: a simple, obviously correct version of the same API, about 1% of the real system's size.

Then **property-based testing** generated millions of random operation sequences, including puts, gets, deletes, crashes, restarts and disk failures, and checked that the real system and the model always agreed.

stat.label: reference model's size vs. real ShardStore

takeaway: Correct is easy to state and hard to build. Test the build against the statement.
deeper:
**Why tiny works:** Correctness is easier to state than to implement fast. The model can be a plain in-memory map with none of the log structure, caching or on-disk layout. Small enough to be obviously right.

**How the check runs:**
1. A tool generates a random sequence of operations, including crashes mid-write.
2. Both the real engine and the model run it.
3. Observable results must match.
4. Any mismatch is reported as a failing sequence to debug.

**Humans forget the nasty cases:** Crash halfway through a write, then restart, is exactly the test nobody writes by hand. Random generation writes it for you.

**A third tool for threads:** Model checking of concurrent code explored thread interleavings, targeting crash-consistency and concurrency bugs that random testing rarely hits.

quiz.q: The reference model says a get after put, crash, restart returns the value; the real engine returns nothing. Which one is wrong, and what did the test just find?
quiz.a: The real engine: the model defines correct behavior. The test found a crash-consistency bug, a write that was lost across a crash and restart.

mcq.q: In ShardStore's property-based testing, what counts as a bug?
options: Any case where the real system and the model disagree
Any operation slower in the real system than the model
Any crash that the test harness injects
Any sequence that the model rejects as invalid
mcq.why: The model defines correct behavior. Random sequences run on both, and a mismatch in observable results flags a bug in the real system.

hook: Formal checks usually rot once the specialist who wrote them moves on. What kept ShardStore's alive?
title: Stopped 16 issues, and ordinary engineers maintained it
body:
The SOSP 2021 ShardStore paper reports that lightweight formal methods prevented 16 issues from reaching production, including subtle **crash-consistency** and concurrency bugs.

The second result matters as much: normal engineers, not formal-methods experts, kept the checks updated as features were added. Verification that only experts can maintain decays as the code moves. Checks every engineer extends alongside each feature keep protecting the system.
takeaway: A check nobody maintains is a check that stopped existing.
deeper:
**The worst kind of bug:** A crash-consistency bug can silently lose or corrupt data only after a specific crash at a specific moment. That may happen once in years across a fleet, and be nearly impossible to reproduce afterwards.

**Why non-experts could:** The reference model is written in Rust like the production code and runs as ordinary tests. An engineer adding a feature adds the simple version of it to the model, and the existing random tests start exercising it immediately.

**The real lesson:** It is cost, not math. A reference model that is 1% of the code and runs in CI every day beats a perfect proof nobody maintains.

**Where it fits:** Parity protects against disks. Checks like these protect against the software bugs behind most real data loss.

quiz.q: Your storage engine has a formal proof written two years ago by a contractor. Since then, 40 features shipped and nobody touched the proof. How much should it reassure you?
quiz.a: Little. It describes the old design, not today's code. Checks only protect code they evolve with; ShardStore's worked because ordinary engineers updated them with every feature.

mcq.q: What did the ShardStore paper report about who maintained its checks?
options: Normal engineers kept them updated as features were added
A dedicated formal-methods team rewrote them each release
They were frozen after launch to avoid false alarms
An external auditor re-verified them every year
mcq.why: Non-specialist engineers extended the checks alongside new features, which is why the approach kept working as the code changed.

hook: One question in a storage design review reveals whether a team can find its own crash bugs. What is it?
title: Ask every storage team: what is your executable spec?
body:
Full proofs are rare for a reason: they are expensive, and hard to keep current as the code changes. The ShardStore lesson is about cost, not math. A reference model that is 1% of the code and runs in CI every day beats a perfect proof that nobody maintains.

So in a review of any new storage engine, ask: **what is your executable spec**, and how do you check the real code against it under crashes? A team without an answer is trusting hand-written tests to find timing bugs.
takeaway: A spec you can run beats a proof you can't maintain.
deeper:
**It forces three answers:**
1. Has the team written down, in runnable form, what correct means? Often it lives only in people's heads, where nobody can check it.
2. Do they test failure, not just success? Storage bugs hide in crash and restart paths, disk errors and concurrent operations.
3. Are the checks cheap enough to survive? A method that needs a specialist, or takes days to run, gets skipped under deadline pressure and rots.

**A good answer:** An executable model in the production language, random operation sequences that include crashes and disk failures, and model checking of concurrent code, all running as part of normal development.

**Why it's a durability question:** Coding schemes protect against hardware. Formal checks on storage code protect against the software bugs behind most real data loss.

quiz.q: A team presenting a new log-structured engine says, 'We have 2,000 unit tests and 95% coverage.' What do you ask next, and why isn't coverage enough?
quiz.a: Ask for their executable spec and how they check the engine against it under crashes and concurrency. Coverage counts lines run, not correctness after a crash at the wrong instant.

mcq.q: Why does the ShardStore lesson favor a 1% reference model over a full proof?
options: It runs in CI daily and evolves with the code
It proves correctness more rigorously than a proof
It removes the need for any crash testing
It is written only by formal-methods specialists
mcq.why: A maintained, runnable model keeps checking the real code as it changes; an unmaintained perfect proof stops matching the system.

hook: Your Spark job writes its output files, lists the folder, and some are missing. No error. What happened?
title: For its first 14 years, S3 could show you stale results
body:
For its first 14 years, S3 was **eventually consistent** for some operations. A `PUT` that overwrote an existing key, or a `LIST` right after a `PUT`, could return old results for a short time.

That broke Hadoop and Spark, which expect to see files they just wrote. Users bolted on extra layers, such as Netflix's s3mper and the EMRFS consistent view, that tracked every write in a separate database to catch stale answers.
takeaway: A stale read with no error is worse than a failed read.
deeper:
**Why web apps shrugged:** A user who uploads a photo rarely notices if a list is briefly out of date.

**Why pipelines broke:** A job that writes output files and then lists the directory might miss some, and a downstream job then processes incomplete data, silently. An overwrite followed by a read might return the old contents: wrong results, no error.

**How the workarounds worked:**
1. Record every write in a separate, strongly consistent database.
2. Compare what S3 returns against that record.
3. Wait or retry when they disagree.

**The catch:** They worked, but cost money, added operational burden, and created a second source of truth that could itself drift. That history is why the December 2020 switch to strong consistency mattered so much to the data ecosystem.

quiz.q: Before 2020, a nightly job overwrote `report.csv` on S3 and a second job read it seconds later. Occasionally the report showed the previous day's numbers. Why, and how did teams defend against it?
quiz.a: An overwrite followed by a read could return the old object for a short time. Teams tracked writes in a separate consistent database, like s3mper or EMRFS consistent view, and retried until S3 matched.

mcq.q: What did tools like s3mper and the EMRFS consistent view do?
options: Tracked writes in a separate database to catch stale results
Cached S3 objects locally to make reads faster
Replicated S3 buckets to a second region for safety
Added hash prefixes to keys to avoid hot partitions
mcq.why: They recorded every write elsewhere, compared S3's answers to that record, and waited or retried when S3 was stale.

hook: For 14 years S3 could hand back stale reads. In 2020 that ended. What had been hiding fresh data?
title: Dec 2020: S3 went strongly consistent for free
body:
In December 2020, S3 became **strongly consistent** for all GET, PUT, LIST and DELETE operations, at no extra cost and with no performance change.

The obstacle had been a **metadata cache**. It made reads fast but could return a stale view after an overwrite. Removing it would have hurt performance at S3's scale. So AWS kept the cache and built a cache coherence protocol that lets it learn when its view is stale.
takeaway: Don't delete the fast path. Teach it to notice when it's wrong.
deeper:
**What strong means here:** Read-after-write. Once a PUT or DELETE succeeds, every later GET and LIST reflects it.

**The cache was the culprit:** Caching metadata is how a system serving over 100 million requests per second keeps its index from being hammered by repeat lookups. But a cache that hears about changes late is exactly what produces eventual consistency.

**Two options, both rejected:**
1. Drop the cache: every read hits the index, a big performance and cost hit.
2. Keep the cache as is: the consistency gap stays.

**The third path:** A coherence protocol keeps the cache on the read path but gives it a cheap way to check freshness, through a new component called the witness. Customers got a stronger guarantee without paying for it in latency or price.

quiz.q: A junior engineer says, 'S3 was eventually consistent because of slow storage replication; they must have added more replicas in 2020.' Correct them.
quiz.a: The staleness came from the metadata cache in front of the index, not storage. AWS kept the cache and added a coherence protocol so it could detect stale entries.

mcq.q: Why didn't AWS simply remove S3's metadata cache to fix consistency?
options: It would have hurt read performance at S3's scale
The cache held the only copy of the metadata
Removing it would have broken bucket versioning
The index could not answer LIST requests without it
mcq.why: The cache shields the index from repeat lookups. AWS kept its speed and added a coherence protocol so it learns when it is stale.

predict.q: In December 2020, S3 became strongly consistent. What did customers pay for it?
options: Nothing extra, and no performance change
A higher price per request
Slightly higher read latency

hook: S3's cache holds version 1 of a key. Version 2 was just written. How does the cache find out in time?
title: The witness: a tiny in-memory check that ended stale reads
body:
S3's fix centers on a new component, the **witness**, which tracks changes to object metadata. On a read, the metadata cache checks with the witness, which acts as a **read barrier**: it tells the cache whether its view of the object is stale. If a newer version exists, the cache fetches it before answering.

The witness keeps only in-memory state, so the check is fast enough for every request.
takeaway: You don't need the latest data to know you're stale, just the latest version.
deeper:
**The sequence:**
1. A writer sends PUT key v2; the index store commits v2.
2. The witness notes a new version for that key.
3. A reader sends GET key. The cache holds v1 and asks the witness whether v1 is still latest.
4. The witness says no; the cache fetches v2 and returns it.

**Why it's small:** The witness does not hold the objects. It only needs enough to answer 'is this view current?', so it lives entirely in memory.

**Who pays:** A cache hit the witness confirms stays fast. Only stale entries pay the extra fetch. Caching keeps its benefit, and the window that caused eventual consistency closes.

**The catch:** A barrier is only as good as the order it enforces. S3 needed a clear per-object order of writes for the witness to be right.

quiz.q: Most GETs hit a cache entry that is still current. What extra work does the witness add for those, and what extra work for a stale one?
quiz.a: Current entries pay only a quick in-memory freshness check. Stale entries also pay a fetch of the newer version before answering.

mcq.q: What role does S3's witness play on a read?
options: A read barrier that tells the cache if its view is stale
A second cache that serves the newest object bytes
A lock that blocks reads while a PUT is in flight
A log that replays missed writes into the index
mcq.why: The witness tracks metadata changes in memory. The cache checks it on reads and refetches only if a newer version exists.

hook: Proving S3's consistency fix correct took more work than building it. Why would AWS spend that much?
title: Proving S3's consistency fix took more work than coding it
body:
For the witness to be right, every component must agree which write to an object is latest. S3 needed a clear **per-object order** of operations. Rather than build one, AWS reused its existing replication logic, originally built for event notifications and cross-region replication.

Then AWS verified the coherence algorithm with **deductive proofs** and model checking, and said the verification work was larger than the implementation work.
takeaway: For core storage correctness, the proof is the product; the code is the easy part.
deeper:
**Why order is everything:** If two PUTs to one key could be seen in different orders by the witness and the index, the witness might vouch for an older version. Strong consistency would fail silently, with no error anywhere.

**Why reuse beat rewrite:** The replication machinery already had to establish per-object order to deliver notifications and cross-region copies correctly. The order S3 needed already existed.

**Why verify so hard:** Consistency protocols are easy to get subtly wrong. Their bugs appear only under rare interleavings of concurrent reads, writes and failures, the cases tests almost never hit. Deductive proofs covered the algorithm; model checking explored its behaviors.

**The same stance twice:** ShardStore's lightweight formal methods and this proof share one view: at the core of a storage system, showing it is correct is the main job.

quiz.q: Suppose the witness and the index could see two PUTs to one key in different orders. Describe the bug a reader would hit.
quiz.a: The witness could tell a cache that an older version is current, so the reader gets stale data with no error, the exact failure strong consistency was meant to remove.

mcq.q: Where did S3 get the per-object ordering its witness needed?
options: It reused existing replication logic
It added a global clock to every server
It sent all writes through one leader
It trusted timestamps set by each client
mcq.why: Replication logic built for event notifications and cross-region replication already ordered each object's operations, so AWS reused it.

hook: GCS is strongly consistent. So why might a user still get an old photo, or a stale permission?
title: 'Strongly consistent' always has a scope. Read the scope.
body:
Google Cloud Storage has long offered strong global consistency for read-after-write, read-after-delete and listing. Its documentation still lists two exceptions. Objects cached by **public caches** can be stale until their cache lifetime ends. **IAM permission changes** are eventually consistent and typically take about a minute.

S3 has eventually consistent corners too, such as bucket configuration changes. A strong consistency label covers a named set of operations, never everything.
takeaway: Bugs live at the edges of guarantees. Find the edges first.
deeper:
**Where it breaks in practice:** An app correctly assumes a new object is readable at once, then fails because a permission granted seconds earlier hasn't propagated. Or a public cache still serves the old copy. Or code changes an S3 bucket's configuration and immediately depends on the new behavior.

**The habit:** Read a provider's consistency docs as two lists, covered operations and exceptions. Map every critical path in your app onto both.

**Designing around the gaps:**
1. Permissions: expect delay; retry with backoff or verify before proceeding.
2. External caches: control freshness with cache lifetimes, or write each version to a new key, which is easy with immutable objects.
3. Configuration: don't chain a config change and a dependent action with no wait.

**The one-liner:** 'Strongly consistent' always has a scope. Read the scope.

quiz.q: Your service grants a new user IAM access to a GCS bucket, then immediately reads an object as that user and gets access denied. Is GCS broken?
quiz.a: No. IAM permission changes are outside GCS's strong consistency scope and typically take about a minute. Retry with backoff or wait before depending on the grant.

mcq.q: Which remains eventually consistent even in Google Cloud Storage?
options: IAM permission changes
Read-after-write on a new object
Read-after-delete on an object
Listing the objects in a bucket
mcq.why: GCS documents strong consistency for reads, deletes and listing, but IAM changes typically take about a minute and public caches can serve stale copies.

hook: S3 is built from hard drives that fail every day. How does it promise you'll almost never lose a file?
title: 11 nines: store 10M objects, lose one per 10,000 years
body:
S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999%, **11 nines**, of annual durability. Store 10 million objects and you can expect to lose one about once every 10,000 years. Yet it is built from hard drives that fail every day.

Four ingredients close the gap: **erasure coding** across Availability Zones, continuous auditing and repair, end-to-end checksums, and engineering process and culture.

stat.label: years per lost object, out of 10 million

takeaway: Make data loss require several failures to line up before repair finishes.
deeper:
**Durability is not availability:** Durability is the chance your data is still intact later. Availability is the chance you can reach it right now. Eleven nines is about the first.

**How the math reads:** Eleven nines means an expected annual loss of about one in 100 billion per object. That is how 10 million objects works out to one loss per 10,000 years. No single drive comes close; the number comes from stacking protections so loss needs several unlikely events to line up before repair catches them.

**Note the word 'designed':** Eleven nines is a design target based on models of failure and repair, not a measured guarantee.

**The catch:** It mainly describes hardware failure. Most real data loss comes from software bugs and human mistakes, which is why process, formal checks and versioning count as part of the durability story, not add-ons.

quiz.q: You store 100 million objects in S3 Standard. Using the 11 nines design target, roughly how often should you expect to lose one?
quiz.a: About once every 1,000 years: ten times more objects than the 10-million example, so losses come ten times as often as once per 10,000 years.

mcq.q: Which set lists S3's four durability ingredients?
options: Erasure coding across AZs, repair, checksums, process
Three replicas, RAID-6, tape backup, checksums
Erasure coding, SSD caching, versioning, geo-replication
Enterprise drives, RAID-6, repair, durability reviews
mcq.why: S3 combines Reed-Solomon across AZs, continuous auditing and repair, end-to-end checksums, and process such as durability reviews.

predict.q: You store 10 million objects in S3 Standard. How often should you expect to lose one?
options: About once every 10,000 years
About once a year
About once a century

hook: Three full copies cost 3× your data. How can S3 survive similar failures while paying far less?
title: Split into k+m shards, lose any m, still read it
body:
S3's first durability ingredient is **Reed-Solomon erasure coding**. An object is split into k data shards plus m **parity shards**, and any k of the k + m can rebuild it. Lose up to m shards and nothing is lost.

Shards go on different drives and hosts and, for regional storage classes, across at least three Availability Zones. AWS does not publish its exact k and m.
takeaway: Parity only protects you if the shards can't fail together.
deeper:
**Cheaper than copies:** Three full copies use 3× raw storage. An erasure code tolerates failures with far less overhead, because parity shards are computed rather than full duplicates. Overhead is (k + m) / k.

**Placement is the other half:** If several shards of one object shared a drive or host, one failure would remove several at once and defeat the math. Spreading shards across drives, hosts and zones keeps failures close to independent, so losing more than m needs unrelated events to coincide.

**Why three zones:** Spreading across at least three Availability Zones means the design aims to survive losing a whole zone. That requirement drives the choice of k and m, and it costs extra parity.

**Why it's cheap here:** Objects are immutable, so parity is computed once at write time and never updated.

quiz.q: A scheme uses k = 10, m = 4, but a buggy placer puts 5 shards of one object on the same host. What's the real fault tolerance for that object?
quiz.a: Worse than advertised: one host failure removes 5 shards, more than m = 4, and the object is lost. Placement, not just k and m, sets real durability.

mcq.q: With k data and m parity shards, what is the storage overhead?
options: (k + m) / k
(k + m) / m
m / k
k × m
mcq.why: You store k + m shards to hold k shards' worth of data, so raw bytes per logical byte is (k + m) / k.

hook: A 9+3 erasure code survives any 3 lost shards. Why does it lose data when one of three zones goes down?
title: 9+3 can't survive losing a zone. 8+4 can.
body:
Take an assumed scheme, not AWS's real numbers: 9 data + 3 parity shards spread evenly over 3 Availability Zones, 4 per zone. Storage **overhead** is 12 / 9 = 1.33×, versus 3× for three full copies.

Now lose a zone. That removes 4 shards, leaving 8, fewer than the 9 needed. The object is gone. An 8 + 4 scheme, overhead 1.5×, leaves exactly 8 after a **zone loss** and survives.
takeaway: Parity must cover your biggest correlated failure, not your average one.
deeper:
**Why zones change the math:** Random drive failures hit scattered shards, so a wide stripe with little parity is fine. A zone outage removes a large, correlated block at once. With shards spread evenly over three zones, one zone takes a third of them. Parity must be at least the number of shards in one zone.

**The quick check:**
1. Overhead = total shards ÷ data shards.
2. Subtract the shards in one zone from the total.
3. It survives a zone loss only if what's left is at least k.

**Still worth it:** Overhead rises from 1.33× to 1.5×. Yet 1.5× is half the cost of three full copies at 3×.

**The caveat:** AWS does not publish its real k and m. These numbers are only for intuition.

quiz.q: With the same even spread over 3 zones, would a 10 data + 5 parity scheme survive losing one zone? Show the numbers.
quiz.a: Yes. 15 shards over 3 zones is 5 per zone; losing one leaves 10, exactly k. Overhead is 15 / 10 = 1.5×.

mcq.q: An 8 data + 4 parity scheme is spread over 3 zones. What is its storage overhead?
mcq.why: 12 total shards ÷ 8 data shards = 1.5×, still half the cost of three full copies.

predict.q: 9 data + 3 parity shards, 4 in each of 3 zones. One zone fails. What happens?
options: The object can't be rebuilt
It survives with one shard to spare
It survives with no shards to spare

hook: Two storage systems use the identical erasure code. One loses data far more often. What's different?
title: Durability is a race against repair, not a code property
body:
S3's second durability ingredient is continuous **auditing and repair**. Background processes constantly read data, verify checksums, and rebuild missing or corrupted shards onto healthy drives.

Durability depends on this speed, not just the coding scheme. Data is at risk only while degraded, between losing a shard and rebuilding it. The faster the repair, the smaller the window for a second and third failure to combine. That makes **repair bandwidth** a first-class design resource.
takeaway: Data is only at risk while it's degraded. Shrink that window.
deeper:
**Where repair time sits:** In a standard durability model, mean time to repair sits in the denominator of mean time to data loss. Shorter repair means rarer loss, without adding any extra storage.

**What the window means:** If a rebuild takes a day, further failures have a day to line up. If it takes an hour, that window is 24× shorter.

**Plan it like customer capacity:** Repair bandwidth, the network and disk capacity kept for rebuilding, has to be budgeted just like capacity for customer traffic.

**Why audit at all:** Not all loss announces itself. A drive can fail loudly, but data can also rot silently through latent sector errors or bit corruption. Only reading data back and checking checksums finds that before a second failure makes it unrecoverable.

quiz.q: Your team can either add one more parity shard per stripe or double repair bandwidth. What does each buy, and what does each cost?
quiz.a: Extra parity tolerates one more simultaneous loss but costs storage on every byte. Faster repair shrinks the degraded window, improving durability without extra storage, but costs reserved network and disk capacity.

mcq.q: Why does faster repair improve durability?
options: It shrinks the window in which further failures can combine
It lets the system use fewer parity shards per stripe
It stops drives from failing in the first place
It moves data to a cheaper, more durable tier
mcq.why: Loss needs extra failures while data is degraded; less repair time means fewer chances. Shorter degraded windows give extra failures less time to line up.

hook: A server's memory flips one bit in your upload. The disk then stores it faithfully. Who notices?
title: Checksum at the client, verify at every hop
body:
S3's third durability ingredient is **end-to-end checksums**. Data is checksummed at upload and verified at many points as it moves through the system and sits on disk. S3 now also lets clients send **additional checksums**, for example CRC-based ones, stored with the object and checked on read.

A checksum is a short fingerprint of the bytes. Change one bit and it no longer matches, so corruption is caught instead of silently served.
takeaway: Protect bytes from the moment they exist, not from the moment they hit disk.
deeper:
**Why 'end to end' matters:** A checksum computed only on disk protects against disk corruption. It does nothing about a bad network card, a memory error in a server, or a software bug that garbles data between hops. A disk-only checksum faithfully protects the wrong bytes. Compute it as early as possible, ideally at the client, and verify at each stage.

**Client checksums close the loop:** The client knows what it meant to upload. S3 stores that fingerprint with the object, and a later read confirms the bytes returned are exactly what was written.

**Two guards, two jobs:** Checksums on the data path catch corruption in flight. Background auditing re-reads stored shards to find silent rot at rest.

**The catch:** Support for newer checksum features varies across S3-compatible systems. Don't assume it; test it.

quiz.q: A storage system checksums data only when writing it to disk. A buggy proxy corrupts an upload before it reaches the storage node. What happens on read?
quiz.a: The corrupted bytes were checksummed as if correct, so every later check passes and bad data is served. Only a checksum computed at the client would reveal the mismatch.

mcq.q: What can S3 clients now send with an upload to strengthen integrity checks?
options: Additional checksums, such as CRC-based ones
A second copy of the object for comparison
A parity shard computed on the client
A signed hash of the bucket's settings
mcq.why: Additional client checksums are stored with the object and checked on read, extending verification all the way from the application.

hook: Before a change ships to S3, its engineers must write one particular list. What's on it?
title: Before shipping, list every way the change could lose data
body:
S3's fourth durability ingredient is process and culture. Andy Warfield describes **durability reviews**: before a change ships, engineers write a threat model listing every way it could lose data and how the design resists each one.

The team also prefers **coarse-grained guardrails**: simple mechanisms that block a whole class of risks, over patching each risk separately. The goal is to make data loss structurally hard, not to fix bugs one at a time.
takeaway: Patch a risk and you fix one bug. Block a class and you fix tomorrow's.
deeper:
**A security review, for data:** Instead of asking 'does it work?', a durability review asks 'how could this destroy data?' A migration that deletes before copying. A garbage collector that misjudges which shards are referenced. A configuration push aimed at the wrong fleet. Writing each threat down forces a concrete defense for each.

**Why coarse beats fine:** Patching every discovered risk leaves you one unforeseen case from an incident. A broad mechanism prevents a whole family of failures, including ones nobody has thought of yet.

**What guardrails look like:** The idea shows up in familiar mechanisms: delaying deletion so a mistake can be undone, or committing an index entry only after data is durable.

**Why process counts as durability:** Hardware redundancy does nothing against a system that faithfully executes a wrong instruction.

quiz.q: Your team found three separate bugs where cleanup jobs deleted live data. Someone proposes three targeted fixes. What would a coarse-grained guardrail look like instead?
quiz.a: One mechanism that blocks the whole class, such as delaying every deletion so it can be undone, rather than fixing each cleanup job's logic separately.

mcq.q: What does an S3 durability review require before a change ships?
options: A threat model of every way the change could lose data
A proof that the change adds no latency
Sign-off that the change passed load testing
A rollback plan for each affected customer
mcq.why: Engineers list every way the change could lose data and how the design resists each, treating data loss like a security threat.

hook: S3 can survive several disks dying at once. What is far more likely to actually lose your data?
title: Most data loss is bugs and people, not three dead disks
body:
Most real data loss is not three disks failing at once. It is **software and people**: a bad deploy, a bug in garbage collection, an operator deleting the wrong thing.

**Coding schemes** protect against hardware. Versioning, delayed deletion, formal checks on storage code and durability reviews protect against people and software. In any design review, ask about both. A review that only asks about the erasure code has covered the less likely half of the risk.
takeaway: Parity protects you from disks. Only process protects you from yourself.
deeper:
**Bugs are perfectly correlated:** The math of k, m and repair time assumes independent hardware failures. A software bug is the opposite. A buggy garbage collector running on every storage node can delete the same class of data everywhere at once. Every shard of every affected object goes together, however much parity you bought.

**The system obeys:** An operator command that deletes a bucket is executed faithfully by a system designed never to lose data. Redundancy copies the instruction, not the judgment.

**Defenses for the likely half:**
1. Versioning: overwrites and deletes can be reversed.
2. Delayed deletion: a window to notice before bytes are gone.
3. Formal checks: crash and concurrency bugs caught before shipping.
4. Durability reviews: every way a change could lose data, written down.

quiz.q: A design doc for a new blob store spends five pages on erasure coding and none on deletes. What two questions do you ask in review?
quiz.a: How is a bad delete or overwrite reversed (versioning, delayed deletion)? How is storage code checked for bugs before deploy (formal checks, durability reviews)? Parity covers neither.

mcq.q: Why can't erasure coding protect against a garbage-collection bug?
options: The bug deletes all shards of an object together
Parity shards are excluded from garbage collection
Garbage collection runs in only one Availability Zone
Erasure coding only protects objects under 1 GB
mcq.why: Parity assumes independent failures. A software bug is correlated and removes every shard at once, so only software and process defenses help.

hook: Hard drives hold vastly more than they did in 2006. Why is S3 running out of something anyway?
title: Drives got bigger, not faster: 1 IOPS per 2 TB
body:
A hard drive does about 120 random I/Os per second, and that number has barely moved since 2006, while capacity has grown enormously. Andy Warfield's point: if drives get bigger but not faster, the I/O available per terabyte keeps falling.

At today's sizes, spreading random I/O evenly gives roughly 1 I/O per second per 2 TB. So S3's scarce resource is not bytes. It is I/O per byte, which Warfield calls **heat**.
takeaway: On hard drives, bytes are cheap. The ability to read them is not.
deeper:
**Why the ratio keeps worsening:** Random I/O is limited by moving parts: seeking the head and waiting for the platter to spin. Those limits haven't improved. Capacity keeps rising. Divide a fixed I/O budget by more terabytes each year and every terabyte gets less.

**The inverted intuition:** You'd think the job is storing bytes cheaply. But bytes are abundant; random reads are what runs out. A drive full of popular data can be overwhelmed while it still has free space.

**Worse every year:** The same hot data now shares fewer I/Os, so placement must spread load more carefully.

**Everyone hit this wall:** Meta's Haystack ran out of IOPS with capacity to spare. Google's Colossus serves hot data from flash.

quiz.q: A team moves the same hot dataset from 4 TB drives to 20 TB drives, using one-fifth as many drives. Random IOPS per drive is unchanged. What happens to read latency, and why?
quiz.a: It gets worse. Total random I/O drops about 5× with one-fifth the drives, while demand is unchanged. I/O per byte, not capacity, was the real limit.

mcq.q: What does Warfield mean by 'heat' in S3?
options: I/O demand per byte stored
Drive temperature under heavy load
The share of objects read each day
Network bandwidth per storage node
mcq.why: With about 120 random IOPS per drive and growing capacity, I/O per byte is the scarce resource; Warfield calls it heat.

predict.q: Since 2006, how much faster have hard drives become at random I/O?
options: Barely at all: still about 120 per second
About 10× faster
About 100× faster

hook: One overloaded drive can slow S3 requests that have nothing else in common. How does S3 make that rare?
title: One customer's workload, served by over a million disks
body:
Put too many hot objects on one drive and it becomes a **hotspot**. Its delays amplify up through the layers of the storage stack as **tail latency**, the slow responses at the far end of the distribution.

S3's first answer is very wide placement. New objects, and the objects inside any single bucket, are spread across a very large number of drives. A single customer can burst across a huge part of the fleet instead of saturating a few disks.

stat.label: disks serving a single customer workload

takeaway: Spread data wide enough and a hotspot becomes a rounding error.
deeper:
**Why one slow drive spreads:** A single request often depends on several shards or internal calls. If one shard sits on an overloaded drive, the whole read waits for the slowest piece.

**Why hoping doesn't work:** At S3's scale, some drive somewhere is always busy. The only fix is making it very unlikely that many hot objects share one drive.

**What wide placement buys:** Because a bucket's objects are scattered widely, a customer with a sudden spike draws I/O from a vast pool of disks, not the handful a naive layout would use. Warfield describes one customer workload served by over a million individual disks.

**The catch:** That parallelism exists only in a fleet this large. A private cluster can't spread one workload over a million disks, because it doesn't have them.

quiz.q: In a small cluster, one bucket's objects all live on 20 drives. A viral post makes that bucket hot. Contrast what happens there with S3's wide placement.
quiz.a: The 20 drives saturate and tail latency spikes for everything on them. In S3, the bucket spans a huge number of drives, so the spike becomes a small extra load spread thinly across the fleet.

mcq.q: Why can one overloaded drive slow many unrelated S3 requests?
options: Reads wait for the slowest shard, and delays amplify up the stack
Every request routes through a single drive's index
The front end pauses all traffic when one drive is slow
Hot drives force the index to split its partitions
mcq.why: A read needing several shards waits for the slowest, and a hotspot's delays amplify up the storage stack as tail latency.

predict.q: Warfield describes one S3 customer workload spread across how many individual disks?
options: Over a million
About a thousand
About ten thousand

hook: Every single workload on S3 is bursty. Why does S3's total demand look smooth and predictable?
title: A million bursty workloads add up to one smooth curve
body:
S3's second answer to heat is **aggregation**. Each workload alone is bursty, with sharp peaks. But when millions share one fleet, their peaks don't line up, and in Warfield's words the aggregate demand smooths and becomes way more predictable.

This **decorrelation effect** is a real economic advantage a small private cluster cannot copy. The third answer is rebalancing: as data cools with age, S3 moves it so each drive holds a mix of hot and cold bytes.
takeaway: A private cluster pays for its own peak. A shared fleet pays for the smoothed sum.
deeper:
**Why it saves money:** A private cluster must be sized for its own peak, even if that peak lasts minutes a day, so most of its I/O sits idle. In a shared fleet, one customer's peak lands in others' quiet periods. The fleet can be sized for the smoother aggregate curve, not the sum of every peak.

**Why wide placement needs it:** Spreading every workload over many drives lets the fleet absorb bursts from pooled headroom. Placement and aggregation work as a pair.

**Rebalancing fixes the slow drift:** New data tends to be hot and old data cold. A drive full of fresh data becomes a hotspot; a drive of only old data wastes its I/O. Moving data so each drive holds a blend keeps demand per drive roughly even.

**The catch:** Leave the shared fleet and you lose this effect, which is why leaving only pays for huge, predictable workloads like Dropbox's.

quiz.q: Your spiky analytics workload peaks at 10× its average. Compare a private cluster with a shared multi-tenant fleet: which needs more idle I/O capacity, and why?
quiz.a: The private cluster: it must be sized for your own 10× peak. In the shared fleet, your peak coincides with others' quiet periods, so capacity is sized for the smooth aggregate.

mcq.q: What is S3's 'decorrelation effect'?
options: Many tenants' peaks don't align, so total demand smooths out
Shards of one object are placed on uncorrelated drives
Hot and cold objects are kept in separate storage classes
Requests are spread by hashing keys across partitions
mcq.why: Each workload is bursty, but millions of them peak at different times, so aggregate demand becomes smoother and more predictable.

hook: Google and Meta hit the same hard-drive wall as S3. Each responded differently. How?
title: Same heat problem: Google adds flash, Meta strands disks
body:
Google's Colossus fights heat with media tiers. Newly written, hot data is spread across all drives and served from flash where it makes sense. Older, colder data moves to larger-capacity drives as it cools. A 2025 Google post describes **L4**, a distributed SSD cache that uses access-pattern analysis to decide what goes on flash.

Meta's Tectonic paper describes the same tension split badly: **Haystack** was limited by disk IOPS with spare capacity, and f4 by capacity with spare IOPS.
takeaway: Split hot and cold into separate systems and each strands what the other needs.
deeper:
**Same physics, three answers:** Hard drives have abundant capacity and scarce random I/O. S3 leans on wide placement, aggregation across tenants, and rebalancing so every drive holds a mix of hot and cold bytes.

**Google moves data between media:** Hot data gets flash, where random I/O is plentiful. Cold data drifts to the biggest drives, where low I/O per terabyte doesn't matter because nobody reads it. L4 adds access-pattern analysis to the choice.

**Meta's cautionary split:** Haystack held hot photos and ran out of disk IOPS long before it filled up. f4 held warm data and filled up while its IOPS sat idle. Each system stranded one resource.

**The fix, later:** Tectonic merged them into one shared filesystem so hot and cold tenants use the same drives' I/O and capacity, the same goal as S3's hot-and-cold mix per drive.

quiz.q: Your hot-photo cluster runs at 95% IOPS and 40% capacity; your archive cluster at 90% capacity and 10% IOPS. What's wrong, and what did Meta do in the same situation?
quiz.a: Each cluster strands the resource the other needs. Meta consolidated Haystack, f4 and more into Tectonic, one shared system where hot tenants use the I/O and cold tenants the capacity.

mcq.q: How does Google's Colossus handle hot versus cold data?
options: Hot data on flash where useful; cold data moves to larger drives
Hot data in a separate cluster; cold data XOR-coded across regions
All data on flash, with drives used only for backups
Cold data deleted after 90 days unless it is re-read
mcq.why: Colossus serves hot data from flash where it makes sense and moves colder data to higher-capacity drives; L4 uses access patterns to choose.

hook: S3 allows unlimited prefixes, yet your app gets 503 Slow Down. Which limit did you hit?
title: 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second, per prefix
body:
S3 automatically partitions its index by key range. AWS documents at least 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE and 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per **partitioned prefix**, with no limit on the number of prefixes. Ten prefixes give roughly ten times the read rate.

Scaling is gradual. While S3 splits partitions to absorb growing load, clients may see `503 Slow Down`. For very high rates, spread keys over many prefixes, and always retry 503s with **exponential backoff and jitter**.
takeaway: S3's limit isn't per bucket. It's per key range, so shape your keys.
deeper:
**Why prefixes matter:** The index is a sorted map split into ranges. Requests for keys in one range all hit the same partition, which has a finite request rate. When a range heats up, S3 splits it into more partitions, each with its own budget. The split takes time, and meanwhile some requests get throttled.

**Spread on purpose:** Put a short hash early in the key, like `a7/photos/user-123/...`, so load lands on many ranges naturally.

**Retry the right way:**
1. Wait after a 503 instead of retrying at once.
2. Grow the wait after each failure (exponential backoff).
3. Add randomness (jitter) so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep.

**The catch:** A hash prefix spreads load but breaks listing by date. Keep an index or table format that records which keys belong to which day.

quiz.q: A service needs 30,000 GETs per second from one bucket, all under the single prefix `images/`. What do you expect, and what do you change?
quiz.a: 503 Slow Down while S3 splits partitions, since the baseline is 5,500 GETs per partitioned prefix. Add a short hash early in the key to spread load, and retry with backoff and jitter.

mcq.q: What baseline does AWS document for GET/HEAD requests per partitioned prefix?
options: At least 5,500 per second
At least 3,500 per second
At least 1,000 per second
At least 100,000 per second
mcq.why: AWS documents at least 5,500 GET/HEAD and 3,500 PUT/COPY/POST/DELETE per second per partitioned prefix, with unlimited prefixes.

hook: A log pipeline's tidy S3 key names cap its write throughput, and the cap returns every day. What's wrong?
title: Date-first keys pour a whole day into one partition
body:
A write-heavy log pipeline names every key `yyyy-mm-dd/...`. It looks tidy. But S3 partitions its index by key range, so all of a day's writes land in one narrow range: one **hot partition**, until S3 splits it.

Throughput collapses to that partition's limit, and clients see `503 Slow Down`. The fix is to put a **hash or shard component** early in the key, and retry 503s with backoff.
takeaway: In a range-partitioned store, key design is performance design.
deeper:
**Do the math:** At 20,000 writes per second, against a baseline of at least 3,500 per partitioned prefix, one day's range is several times over budget. Writes throttle until S3 splits the range, and may still exceed per-prefix limits.

**It comes back daily:** At midnight, every write moves to a brand new date range that hasn't been split yet. The hot spot doesn't go away; it moves.

**The fix:**
1. Add a short hash or shard number before the date, like `a7/2026-09-26/...`.
2. Retry 503s with exponential backoff and jitter.
3. Record which keys belong to which day in an index or table format, instead of listing by date prefix.

**The general rule:** Sequential key prefixes, like dates, concentrate load on one range in any range-partitioned store.

quiz.q: After fixing their keys to `00/` through `ff/` then the date, an analyst asks for 'all logs from March 3'. How do they find them without a full bucket scan?
quiz.a: From a separate index or table format that maps each day to its keys, written at ingest. With hash-first keys, listing by a date prefix no longer works.

mcq.q: Why do date-first keys hurt a write-heavy S3 pipeline?
options: All of a day's writes hit one key range and index partition
S3 rejects keys that begin with a numeric date
Date prefixes disable S3's automatic partition splitting
Listing becomes unsorted when keys start with dates
mcq.why: S3 partitions its index by key range. A shared date prefix funnels every write into one hot partition until S3 splits it.
