hook: You need every key in a bucket holding a billion objects. How much work can simply listing them take?
title: Listing a billion objects takes a million calls
body:
`ListObjectsV2` returns keys in lexicographic (UTF-8 binary) order, up to 1,000 per page, with a **continuation token** for the next page. A billion-object bucket needs about a million mostly sequential calls.

That is why big data systems avoid 'list the directory to find the files'. Table formats like Apache Iceberg keep an explicit **manifest** of files instead. For large audits, **S3 Inventory** delivers a daily or weekly file listing every object.
takeaway: Don't discover your files by listing. Keep a list.
deeper:
**Why it's sequential:** Each page's continuation token says where the next one starts, so a naive client must wait for page N before asking for page N+1. Call count grows linearly with object count, and even fast calls add up to long runtimes and real request costs.

**Why table formats keep manifests:** Iceberg and similar formats record exactly which data files make up each snapshot. A query engine reads a few metadata files instead of listing thousands of prefixes.

**Audits go offline:** S3 Inventory turns 'list everything live' into 'process a periodic report file'.

**The catch:** Directory buckets in S3 Express One Zone have a real hierarchy, and their list results are not sorted. Code that assumes sorted listing can break there.

quiz.q: A nightly job lists a 3-billion-object bucket to count objects per prefix, and it never finishes before morning. What should it use instead?
quiz.a: S3 Inventory: a daily or weekly file listing all objects, processed offline, instead of about 3 million sequential list calls.

mcq.q: Why does listing a huge S3 bucket take so many calls?
options: Each page returns at most 1,000 keys, fetched in sequence
Each call returns only the keys under one folder
Listing must read every object's data to verify it
Keys come back in random order and need de-duplication
mcq.why: ListObjectsV2 pages hold up to 1,000 keys with a continuation token, so a billion objects means about a million calls.

predict.q: About how many ListObjectsV2 calls does it take to list a billion-object bucket?
options: About 1 million
About 1,000
About 1 billion

hook: Most of your photos haven't been opened in years, yet you pay hot prices. Which ones must stay hot anyway?
title: One API, many price tiers: move photos after 90 days
body:
S3 puts the same object API on top of different physical tiers called **storage classes**. They trade storage price against request price, minimum storage duration and retrieval time.

For the photo app, a **lifecycle rule** could move photos older than 90 days to a cheaper class while keeping profile photos hot. Most photos cool with age. Profile photos are the exception, so they stay in the hot class whatever their age.
takeaway: Tier by the access curve, and know which data breaks it.
deeper:
**The API hides the tier:** A `GET` looks the same whether the bytes sit on hot drives or in an archive. Latency and price differ; the code doesn't. So you optimize cost with lifecycle rules, not code changes.

**Same insight as Meta's f4:** Data cools with age, so older content can live somewhere cheaper. Meta's f4 likewise never moved profile photos.

**Where tiering backfires:**
1. Data still read often: in an infrequent-access class, retrieval and request charges can outweigh the storage savings.
2. Early deletes: move or delete before the minimum duration and you still pay for the full period.

**When you can't predict:** Intelligent-Tiering is for unknown or changing access. It has no minimum duration, millisecond access, and optional slower archive tiers.

quiz.q: A team moves every object older than 30 days to Standard-IA to save money, but the bill goes up. A dashboard reads that data daily. What happened?
quiz.a: Standard-IA trades lower storage price for higher request and retrieval cost. Daily reads rack up charges that outweigh the storage savings; the data belongs in Standard or Intelligent-Tiering.

mcq.q: What do S3 storage classes trade against each other?
options: Storage price vs. request price, minimum duration and retrieval time
Durability vs. the number of objects allowed per bucket
Encryption strength vs. storage price
Maximum object size vs. retrieval time
mcq.why: Every class exposes the same API; they differ in storage price, request price, minimum storage duration and time to first byte.

hook: Delete a Glacier Deep Archive object after one week. How long are you billed for?
title: S3 classes: milliseconds to 12 hours, 0 to 180 days
body:
Eight classes, three dials: zones, minimum duration, first-byte latency. Standard, Intelligent-Tiering and Standard-IA span 3 or more Availability Zones with millisecond access; Standard-IA adds a 30-day **minimum storage duration**. One Zone-IA: one zone, 30 days, re-creatable copies. Express One Zone: one zone, single-digit ms, ML and analytics scratch.

Glacier Instant Retrieval: milliseconds, 90 days. Glacier Flexible Retrieval: minutes to hours, 90 days. **Glacier Deep Archive**: within 12 hours, 180 days, compliance archives. Delete early and you still pay the minimum.
takeaway: Zones buy resilience, minimums reveal intent, latency separates online from archive.
deeper:
**Dial one, zones:** One Zone-IA and Express One Zone keep data in a single Availability Zone, so they suit data you can re-create, or that needs locality more than resilience. Every other class spans 3 or more zones.

**Dial two, minimum duration:** None for Standard and Intelligent-Tiering, 30 days for the IA classes, 90 days for Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, 180 days for Deep Archive. The minimum signals the intended use. Delete early and you pay the rest anyway.

**Dial three, first-byte latency:** Standard-IA and Glacier Instant Retrieval are cheaper but still online, in milliseconds. Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, Deep Archive within 12 hours. Those fit only data you can wait for.

**Typical uses:** Standard for hot data, Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access, Standard-IA for backups read monthly, Glacier Instant Retrieval for archives read rarely but fast.

quiz.q: You need monthly-readable backups that must survive an AZ outage, plus thumbnail caches you can regenerate. Pick a class for each.
quiz.a: Backups: Standard-IA, multi-AZ with millisecond access and a 30-day minimum. Thumbnails: One Zone-IA, since they are re-creatable and an AZ loss only costs regeneration.

mcq.q: Which S3 class has a 180-day minimum and first-byte latency within 12 hours?
options: Glacier Deep Archive
Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Glacier Instant Retrieval
S3 One Zone-IA
mcq.why: Deep Archive is the slowest tier: within 12 hours to first byte, a 180-day minimum, aimed at compliance archives.

hook: AWS built an S3 that's up to 10× faster by giving up something S3 is famous for. What?
title: Express One Zone: up to 10× faster, in a single AZ
body:
Launched November 28, 2023, **S3 Express One Zone** stores data in a single Availability Zone on purpose-built hardware, in a new bucket type called a **directory bucket**. AWS claims up to 10× faster access than S3 Standard, consistent single-digit millisecond latency, and request costs up to 80% lower.

The price is resilience: an AZ failure can make data unavailable or, in a disaster, lost. It targets ML training loaders, interactive analytics and other many-small-request workloads.
takeaway: One zone is closer and faster, and one disaster away from gone.
deeper:
**How it differs:**
1. Single AZ: put compute in the same zone to cut network latency.
2. Session auth: `CreateSession` returns a token valid for five minutes, so each request skips full IAM authorization.
3. Real directories: directory buckets have a hierarchical namespace, unlike general purpose buckets.

**The porting catch:** Listing in directory buckets is not sorted. Code written for S3 Standard that assumes sorted listings can break.

**When to pick it:** Latency or request cost dominates, such as ML data loading or many small reads from compute in one AZ.

**What you give up:** Multi-AZ resilience, plus some familiar API behavior: directory buckets, unsorted listing, session auth. It is one of three recent launches, with Tables and Vectors, that pull in workloads that used to need a separate system.

quiz.q: Your training cluster runs in one AZ and reads millions of small files per epoch from S3 Standard; the dataset is a copy of a master kept elsewhere. Move it to Express One Zone? What's the risk?
quiz.a: Yes: many small same-AZ reads are its target, with lower latency and request cost. The risk is an AZ event making the copy unavailable or lost, acceptable because the master exists elsewhere.

mcq.q: How does S3 Express One Zone avoid full IAM authorization on every request?
options: CreateSession issues a short-lived five-minute token
It skips authentication for same-AZ clients
It caches bucket policies inside each client SDK
It authorizes only the first request per connection
mcq.why: A session token from CreateSession, valid for five minutes, lets requests avoid paying the full IAM authorization cost each time.

hook: Running Iceberg on S3 means babysitting background jobs forever. What did AWS take off your plate in 2024?
title: S3 Tables: the bucket now understands tables
body:
Launched December 3, 2024, **S3 Tables** added a third bucket type, the **table bucket**, which stores Apache Iceberg tables. S3 runs the maintenance for you: compacting small files to a target size configurable between 64 and 512 MiB, expiring snapshots, and removing unreferenced files.

AWS claims up to 3× faster queries and up to 10× more transactions per second than self-managed Iceberg tables in general purpose buckets. Object storage is moving up the stack, from bytes by key to tables.
takeaway: When storage understands your data's shape, it can maintain it for you.
deeper:
**What Iceberg is:** A table format that stores data as files in object storage, plus metadata tracking which files belong to each snapshot.

**Chores you used to own:** Get any of these wrong and you hurt performance or waste storage.
1. Compaction: frequent writes pile up small files that slow queries, so they must be merged.
2. Snapshot expiry: old snapshots accumulate and must be removed.
3. Orphan cleanup: files no longer referenced by any snapshot must be deleted, or you keep paying for them.

**Built on earlier pieces:** Conditional writes, added in 2024, already let table formats commit atomically on S3 without an external lock service.

**The strategic shift:** A table becomes something the storage layer understands natively, not a convention each analytics engine maintains on top of anonymous objects.

quiz.q: A team's self-managed Iceberg table gets slower every week and its storage bill keeps rising, though data volume is flat. Which maintenance is probably missing?
quiz.a: Compaction, since small files pile up and slow queries, plus snapshot expiry and unreferenced-file removal, since dead files keep being billed. S3 Tables runs all three.

mcq.q: What target file size can S3 Tables compaction be configured to?
options: Between 64 and 512 MiB
Between 4 and 64 MiB
Between 1 and 5 GiB
Between 512 MiB and 2 GiB
mcq.why: S3 Tables compacts small files to a configurable target of 64 to 512 MiB, and also expires snapshots and removes unreferenced files.

hook: Why would you choose a vector store whose queries take around 100 ms, even up to a second?
title: S3 Vectors: slower search, up to 90% cheaper
body:
S3 Vectors previewed in mid-2025 and became generally available on December 2, 2025. It adds **vector buckets** and vector indexes for embeddings. At GA, AWS listed up to 2 billion vectors per index, up to 20 trillion per vector bucket, and query latency around 100 ms or less for frequent queries, under a second for infrequent ones.

The pitch: a claimed cost cut of up to 90% versus specialized vector databases, for large, rarely queried vector sets.

stat.label: max claimed cost cut vs. specialized vector DBs

takeaway: Don't pay in-memory prices for embeddings you query once a month.
deeper:
**What it searches:** Embeddings are numeric vectors representing content such as text, images or audio. Similarity search finds the vectors closest to a query.

**The trade:** Specialized vector databases target very low-latency online retrieval, which usually means indexes in memory or on fast storage, expensive at large scale. S3 Vectors takes the object storage side: much lower cost per vector, with latency around 100 ms for frequent queries and under a second for infrequent ones.

**Who it's for:** Large, rarely queried vector sets, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) archives or semantic search over media. Not the lowest-latency online retrieval path.

**The familiar shape:** Like photos read for days and then rarely, many embedding collections are queried only occasionally. Paying hot prices for all of them wastes money.

quiz.q: You have live product recommendations on every page view, and semantic search over a huge media archive used a few times a day. Which fits S3 Vectors, and why?
quiz.a: The media archive: large, rarely queried, fine with around 100 ms to a second. Live recommendations need the lowest-latency online retrieval, which S3 Vectors does not target.

mcq.q: At general availability, what per-index scale did AWS list for S3 Vectors?
options: Up to 2 billion vectors
Up to 20 trillion vectors
Up to 100 million vectors
Up to 50 billion vectors
mcq.why: At GA on December 2, 2025, AWS listed up to 2 billion vectors per index and up to 20 trillion per vector bucket.

hook: You're about to adopt a specialized database for one workload. What should you ask about S3 first?
title: Will S3 absorb your specialized store within two years?
body:
Look at S3's recent launches: Express One Zone for lower latency, Tables for structured data, Vectors for similarity search. Each attacks a workload that used to need a **separate system in front of S3**.

So when you choose a specialized store, ask two questions. Will object storage absorb this use case within two years? And what does my team **own** if it does not? The first guards against building something soon redundant; the second makes the ownership cost explicit.
takeaway: Before you adopt a system, price what you'll own if you're wrong.
deeper:
**Half one, the trend:** Object storage keeps moving up the stack, from bytes by key to low-latency buckets, native Iceberg tables and vector indexes. A team that builds its own specialized cluster today may soon find a cheaper managed version in the storage layer, leaving a system to maintain and migrate away from.

**Half two, the bill:** If object storage doesn't absorb it, what exactly do you run? The cluster, upgrades, capacity planning, durability, on-call. Sometimes that is right, for example when you need the lowest online latency, which S3 Vectors does not target. But the cost should be written down, not discovered.

**The same arc elsewhere:** Meta folded specialized systems into Tectonic to stop stranding resources. Dropbox's move off the cloud worked because its workload was simple, huge and predictable.

quiz.q: Your team wants a self-hosted vector database to search a 500-million-embedding archive queried weekly. Apply the two-question test.
quiz.a: Object storage already absorbed this: S3 Vectors targets large, rarely queried sets. Self-hosting means owning cluster ops, upgrades, capacity and on-call for a workload that doesn't need lowest latency.

mcq.q: What pattern links S3 Express One Zone, S3 Tables and S3 Vectors?
options: Each absorbs a workload that once needed a separate system
Each stores its data in a single Availability Zone
Each replaces S3's index layer with a new database
Each was built to cut S3 Standard's storage price
mcq.why: Lower latency, structured tables and similarity search each used to require a separate system in front of S3.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: GFS hit a size ceiling set by its metadata. How did its successor grow more than 100× past it?
title: Colossus: metadata in Bigtable, 100× past GFS
body: Google Cloud Storage sits on **Colossus**, Google's cluster filesystem and the successor to GFS. Google's 2021 description lists four parts. The client library is the most complex: it implements software RAID and encodings chosen per application. **Curators** are the scalable metadata service, storing filesystem metadata in Bigtable, which let Colossus scale more than 100× beyond the largest GFS clusters. D file servers are network-attached disks. Custodians are background workers for durability and balance.
takeaway: Scale the metadata and the bytes will follow.
deeper:
**Smart client, simple servers:** Instead of servers deciding how data is encoded, the client does software RAID and picks encodings per application, so different users get different trade-offs from one fleet. Custodians handle the background work, including RAID reconstruction, like S3's repair and rebalance services.

**Metadata off the data path:** Clients ask curators where data lives, then read and write directly with D file servers. The metadata path stays small; the data path stays wide.

**Why Bigtable mattered:** GFS used a single metadata master, which capped cluster size. Moving metadata into Bigtable, a distributed table store, removed that ceiling.

**How big now:** Google's 2025 update says it runs at least two Colossus filesystems larger than 10 exabytes each, with over 50 TB/s of read and 25 TB/s of write throughput across its fleet.

quiz.q: In Colossus, a client wants to read a file. Which components does it talk to, in order, and which one never carries the file's bytes?
quiz.a: First curators, to learn where the data lives, then D file servers directly for the bytes. Curators, the metadata service, never carry the data itself.

mcq.q: Which Colossus component is described as the most complex?
options: The client library
The curators
The D file servers
The custodians
mcq.why: The client library implements software RAID and per-application encodings, so it carries most of Colossus's complexity.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: S3 built its own storage and index layers from scratch. What does Google Cloud Storage stand on instead?
title: GCS rides shared Google infra: Colossus plus Spanner
body:
In Google's description of the Cloud Storage stack, **Spanner** holds metadata about access permissions and data location. That fits GCS's strong global consistency for object and list operations: a globally consistent database is a natural place to keep the object namespace.

The key difference from S3: GCS is one product built on **shared Google infrastructure**, Colossus for bytes and Spanner for metadata, also used by YouTube, Ads and Compute Engine. S3 is a standalone service with purpose-built layers.
takeaway: Build on shared infrastructure and you inherit its scale and its design choices.
deeper:
**S3 built its own:** ShardStore on the storage nodes, its own sharded index, and in 2020 a witness-based cache coherence protocol to reach strong consistency.

**GCS leans on Spanner:** Strong consistency for reads after writes, deletes and listing fits naturally with metadata in a globally consistent database. Durable bytes come from Colossus, which Google already runs at exabyte scale.

**The platform trade-off:** Shared infrastructure means GCS rides investment and scale driven by the whole company. A purpose-built stack lets S3 tune every layer for object storage, such as heat-aware placement across millions of drives, at the cost of building and verifying more itself.

**The fine print:** Even GCS's strong consistency has a scope. Public caches and IAM permission changes remain eventually consistent.

quiz.q: An architect claims GCS and S3 both 'keep metadata in a globally consistent database'. What's accurate and what isn't?
quiz.a: Accurate for GCS: Spanner holds metadata on permissions and data location. Not for S3: it uses its own sharded index plus a witness-based cache coherence protocol.

mcq.q: What is the main architectural difference between GCS and S3?
options: GCS builds on shared Google infra; S3 has purpose-built layers
GCS is eventually consistent; S3 is strongly consistent
GCS uses replication only; S3 uses erasure coding only
GCS stores metadata with each object; S3 uses an index
mcq.why: GCS uses Colossus and Spanner, shared with YouTube, Ads and Compute Engine; S3 runs ShardStore and its own index.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: Azure moves a customer's whole storage account to another cluster, and no client config changes. How?
title: Azure stamps: 2 PB to 30 PB clusters, kept ~70% full
body:
Microsoft published the design of Windows Azure Storage (WAS) at SOSP 2011. Its unit is the **storage stamp**, a cluster of racks. First-generation stamps held about 2 PB raw; the next generation up to 30 PB. Microsoft aims to keep each stamp around 70% utilized and moves accounts between stamps as one fills.

The **Location Service** maps each storage account to a stamp and updates DNS, so `account.blob.core.windows.net` points at the right stamp. Moving an account is a DNS change.
takeaway: Put a name in front of every cluster and you can move anything behind it.
deeper:
**Unit of scale and failure:** Instead of one giant global cluster, Azure builds many bounded ones, each with its own front ends, partition servers and storage. That caps the blast radius of problems and makes growth concrete: add stamps.

**Why about 70%:** Headroom absorbs bursts, drive failures and rebuilds, and leaves room to accept accounts migrated from fuller stamps.

**DNS as the indirection:** Clients don't hardcode a stamp; they resolve the account name. Moving an account between stamps changes one DNS entry, not every client's configuration.

**Contrast with S3:** S3 spreads each bucket's objects over a very large number of drives across its fleet. Azure binds an account to one stamp, and replication to another stamp provides geo disaster recovery.

quiz.q: An Azure stamp is filling up well past its target. Describe what Microsoft does and why customers don't notice.
quiz.a: It moves some accounts to emptier stamps. The Location Service updates DNS so each account's hostname resolves to its new stamp, with no client configuration change.

mcq.q: In Windows Azure Storage, what is a storage stamp?
options: A cluster of racks with its own full storage stack
A single rack of drives behind one front-end server
A DNS record mapping an account to a region
A sealed, immutable chunk of appended data
mcq.why: A stamp is a cluster of racks, about 2 PB raw in the first generation and up to 30 PB later, with its own layers.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: Azure erasure codes its data, but never data that's still being written. What event unlocks the switch?
title: Inside an Azure stamp: extents grow, seal, then freeze
body:
Each stamp has three layers. Stateless front ends authenticate and route to the right partition server. The **partition layer** manages blobs, tables and queues in range partitions, each served by one partition server; strong consistency and per-partition transactions come from here.

The **stream layer** is an append-only distributed filesystem storing data in **extents**. An extent is appended until it reaches a target size, then sealed. A sealed extent is immutable, so cold ones can be erasure coded.
takeaway: Seal it, then encode it: immutability is what makes cheap redundancy safe.
deeper:
**Same shape as S3:** A stateless front end that scales with requests, a metadata and consistency layer, and a byte layer. The stream layer knows nothing about blobs or tables, only append-only streams of extents.

**One server per partition:** Because each range partition is served by a single partition server, that server can order the operations on its keys. That is where strong consistency and transactions within a partition come from.

**Sealing is the trick:**
1. While open, an extent takes appends and is replicated synchronously inside the stamp.
2. At its target size, it is sealed and can never change.
3. Cold sealed extents can later be erasure coded, with parity computed once.

**The same idea at Meta:** Azure's seal-then-erasure-code matches Meta's hot in Haystack, then move to f4.

quiz.q: An engineer proposes erasure coding Azure extents while they're still open for appends, to save space sooner. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: Every append would change the data and force parity to be recomputed. Sealing first makes the extent immutable, so parity is computed once and never touched again.

mcq.q: In WAS, where do strong consistency and per-partition transactions come from?
options: The partition layer
The stream layer
The front-end layer
The Location Service
mcq.why: Each range partition is served by one partition server, which gives strong consistency and transactions per partition.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: Azure copies your write to another region, but doesn't wait for that copy before saying 'done'. Is that safe?
title: Sync inside the stamp, async across regions
body:
WAS uses two kinds of replication with different jobs. **Intra-stamp replication** is synchronous: a write is copied to replicas inside the stamp before it's acknowledged. That gives durability. **Inter-stamp replication** is asynchronous: data is copied to another stamp, typically in another region, after the fact. That gives geographic disaster recovery.

The split keeps write latency low while still guarding against losing a whole site.
takeaway: Wait for what's close; stream to what's far.
deeper:
**Why not sync everywhere:** Synchronous cross-region replication would make every write wait for a long-distance round trip. Keeping sync replicas close means fast acks, and an acknowledged write still survives failures inside the cluster.

**What async costs:** The remote copy lags slightly. A sudden regional disaster could lose the most recent writes that hadn't shipped yet. That is the trade for fast writes.

**Cheaper over time:** Inside the stamp, the stream layer can later erasure code cold sealed extents, cutting the overhead of synchronous replicas for data that no longer changes.

**A different choice:** Dropbox Magic Pocket stores each block in at least two geographic zones, with cross-zone replication within about one second of upload.

quiz.q: A region hosting an Azure stamp is destroyed seconds after a customer's write was acknowledged. Is that write guaranteed to exist in the other region?
quiz.a: No. Inter-stamp replication is asynchronous, so the most recent writes may not have shipped. The acknowledgment only guaranteed synchronous replicas inside the lost stamp.

mcq.q: Which WAS replication is synchronous, and what does it provide?
options: Intra-stamp; durability
Inter-stamp; durability
Intra-stamp; geo disaster recovery
Inter-stamp; geo disaster recovery
mcq.why: Replicas inside a stamp are written before the ack, for durability. Copies to another stamp are asynchronous, for geo disaster recovery.

section: 3.3 Google Cloud Storage and Azure Blob Storage
hook: S3, Azure and Colossus all ended up with the same two-layer shape. What is it, and why does it keep winning?
title: Every big object store: small smart index, big dumb bytes
body:
Look across S3, Windows Azure Storage and Colossus and one pattern repeats: a **separate metadata or index layer** over an append-only or immutable data layer, with **erasure coding** applied once data is sealed. The Azure paper's 'seal then erasure code' is the same idea as Meta's 'hot in Haystack, then move to f4'.

The split separates the hard coordination problem from the bulk byte-storage problem, so each can use the right tools.
takeaway: Coordinate the small records; never coordinate the bytes.
deeper:
**Two very different problems:** Metadata needs consistency, ordering and fast lookups, but its records are small. Data is huge in volume but, if immutable, needs almost no coordination. Split them and each layer uses the right tool: a sharded index, Bigtable, Spanner, a partition layer or ZippyDB for metadata; simple append-only storage for bytes.

**Durability gets cheaper with age:**
1. New data stays in a fast form, such as replicas, while hot or still being assembled.
2. Once sealed, it converts to an erasure-coded form with much lower overhead.
3. Parity is computed once, because the data never changes again.

**Where the arc shows up:** Azure's sealed extents, Meta's move from Haystack's 3.6× to f4's 2.1×, and Dropbox's replicate-first, erasure-code-later design.

**The shared commit rule:** Write the data first, then record it in the metadata layer.

quiz.q: You're designing a blob store. An intern proposes erasure coding every write immediately, including half-assembled uploads. What's the standard pattern instead, and why?
quiz.a: Replicate new data while it's hot or still being assembled, then erasure code it once sealed. Sealed data is immutable, so parity is computed once instead of on every change.

mcq.q: Which pair shows the same 'seal, then erasure code' idea?
options: Azure's sealed extents and Meta's Haystack-to-f4 move
S3's witness and GCS's Spanner metadata
MinIO's erasure sets and Ceph's bucket index
Backblaze tomes and S3's key prefixes
mcq.why: Azure erasure codes cold sealed extents; Meta moves cooled photos from replicated Haystack to erasure-coded f4. Both encode data once it stops changing.

hook: Facebook's 2010 photo store had disk bandwidth to spare and still choked. What was eating its disks?
title: 260 billion photos, and the disks were busy reading inodes
body:
In 2010, Facebook stored over 260 billion images (more than 20 PB), took in about one billion new photos (about 60 TB) a week, and served over one million images per second at peak. Each upload was stored in four sizes.

The first design used NAS appliances over NFS, one file per image. Reading one photo took several disk operations: filename to **inode**, read the inode, then read the data. **Disk seeks**, not bandwidth, were the bottleneck.
takeaway: If finding the data costs more I/O than reading it, fix the finding.
deeper:
**The read path:**
1. One or more disk operations to translate the filename to an inode.
2. One to read the inode.
3. One to read the photo itself.
With a naive directory layout, a single read could take more than 10 disk operations.

**Fatal on hard drives:** A drive offers only about 120 random operations per second. Spending most of them on filesystem bookkeeping wastes the scarcest resource. Four sizes per upload made it worse: each size is another file with its own inode and directory entry.

**Why caching didn't save it:** Metadata caching helps only if it fits in memory. With hundreds of billions of files, general filesystem metadata was far too large.

**A long arc begins:** Haystack (OSDI 2010) attacked exactly this overhead, and f4 and Tectonic followed.

quiz.q: A file-per-image store needs 4 disk operations per photo read, and each drive does about 120 random I/Os per second. Roughly how many photos per second can one drive serve, and what would one operation per read give?
quiz.a: About 30 photos per second at 4 operations each, versus about 120 at one operation per read: roughly 4× more from the same drive.

mcq.q: What limited Facebook's original NFS photo store?
options: Disk seeks spent on metadata before reading data
Network bandwidth between NAS and web servers
Storage capacity of the NAS appliances
CPU cost of resizing each photo four ways
mcq.why: Each read needed separate disk operations for filename-to-inode, the inode and the data, so seeks, not bandwidth, were the bottleneck.

predict.q: What bottlenecked Facebook's original NFS photo store in 2010?
options: Disk seeks spent finding each photo
Network bandwidth to the NAS
Raw storage capacity

hook: How do you read any one of 260 billion photos with at most a single disk operation?
title: Haystack: one disk read per photo, at most
body:
Haystack (OSDI 2010) packed many photos into a few huge files called **physical volumes**, about 100 GB each. Each photo is a **needle** inside a volume: header, key, flags, size, data and checksum.

Each Store machine keeps an **in-memory index** from photo key to (volume, offset, size). A read needs at most one disk operation: seek to the offset and read. The filesystem's metadata lookups are gone from the read path.
takeaway: Put the map in RAM and the disk only reads photos.
deeper:
**Why it fits in RAM:** Per photo it holds only a key and a few numbers, not inodes, directory entries and permissions. That made the whole map small enough for memory.

**Writes are appends:** New needles go to the end of a volume. An update is a new needle with the same key. Deletes set a flag, and compaction later reclaims space.

**Fast restarts, replicas, cache:** An index file per volume lets a machine rebuild its in-memory map quickly after a restart. A Directory maps logical volumes to physical volumes on different machines for replication, and a Cache absorbs hot reads.

**The payoff:** The paper reports each usable terabyte cost about 28% less and served about 4× more reads per second than the NAS setup.

quiz.q: A Haystack Store machine reboots. What would it cost to rebuild its in-memory index by scanning every volume, and what does it do instead?
quiz.a: It would read every ~100 GB volume end to end, a very slow restart. Instead it loads a per-volume index file to rebuild the key-to-offset map quickly.

mcq.q: What does a Haystack Store machine's in-memory index map?
options: Photo key to volume, offset and size
Filename to inode number
Logical volume to physical machines
Photo key to its four resized URLs
mcq.why: Key to (volume, offset, size) lets a read seek straight to the needle with at most one disk operation. The Directory handles logical-to-physical volumes.

hook: Facebook stored every photo at 3.6×, even ones nobody opens. What single measurement changed that?
title: Week-old BLOBs get 10× fewer requests. f4 bet on it.
body:
Haystack kept three replicas, and each Store machine used RAID-6, for an **effective replication factor** of 3.6 (3 × 1.2). Fine for hot data, too expensive for data nobody reads.

Then Meta measured request rates by age. Week-old **BLOBs** had an order of magnitude lower request rate than content under a day old, for eight of nine types studied. Photos became warm after about three months. Profile photos were never moved.
takeaway: Measure the access-by-age curve before you design the tier.
deeper:
**What the curve meant:** If requests drop 10× within a week, most stored bytes are rarely read. Yet under Haystack they all paid for 3.6× raw storage and I/O built for hot traffic.

**What it justified:** A separate warm tier, f4 (OSDI 2014), optimized for low cost per byte instead of high I/O per byte. Once content cools, it moves there.

**Not one rule for everything:** Photos counted as warm after about three months. Profile photos were never moved at all.

**The lesson:** f4 did not win with a clever code. It won by measuring access by age and building a cheaper tier for the long tail. S3 lifecycle rules apply the same idea.

quiz.q: Your video platform wants a cheaper cold tier. Before choosing a coding scheme, what data do you collect, and what result would make you drop the idea?
quiz.a: The request-rate-by-age curve per content type. If access stays flat or unpredictable with age, a warm tier saves little and adds retrieval cost; a steep drop justifies it.

mcq.q: How did Haystack reach an effective replication factor of 3.6?
options: 3 replicas, each on RAID-6 with 1.2× overhead
3.6 full replicas spread across regions
RS(10,4) plus one extra full copy
2 replicas plus 1.6× erasure-coding overhead
mcq.why: Three replicas × RAID-6 overhead of 1.2 per Store machine = 3.6× raw bytes per logical byte.

predict.q: A week after upload, how does a typical Facebook BLOB's request rate compare with its first day?
options: About 10× lower
About the same
About 2× lower

hook: f4 cut storage from 3.6× to 1.4× inside a cell, yet can lose any 4 of 14 blocks. How?
title: f4: Reed-Solomon 10+4, spread across racks, at 1.4×
body:
f4 stores warm BLOBs. Inside a cell, data is encoded with **Reed-Solomon (10,4)**: 10 data blocks plus 4 parity, so any 10 of the 14 rebuild the data. Overhead is 1.4×, against 3.6× in Haystack.

The blocks of each stripe are spread **across racks**, so a rack failure can't take out many blocks of one stripe. In 2014, f4 stored over 65 PB of logical data.
takeaway: Erasure coding is cheapest where reads are rarest.
deeper:
**Why warm data suits it:** Reads are rare, so the extra work of reconstructing a missing block is rarely paid. The capacity savings apply to every stored byte. And cooled data is effectively immutable, so no small edits force parity recomputation.

**Why racks, specifically:** A rack can fail as a unit, through a switch or power problem. If several blocks of one stripe sat in one rack, a single failure could take out more than the four the code tolerates. Rack-aware placement keeps failures close to independent, the same logic S3 applies across drives, hosts and zones.

**The missing piece:** 1.4× protects within one cell, in one region. Surviving a whole-region loss needs another layer. A second full encoded copy elsewhere would double overhead to 2.8×. f4 found a cheaper way, reaching 2.1×.

quiz.q: A bug places 5 blocks of one 10+4 stripe in the same rack. The rack loses power. Is the data safe?
quiz.a: Not while the rack is down: 5 lost blocks leave 9, below the 10 needed. If those drives die, the stripe is gone. Rack-aware placement prevents exactly this.

mcq.q: What is the storage overhead of Reed-Solomon (10,4)?
mcq.why: 14 blocks stored for 10 blocks of data: 14 ÷ 10 = 1.4×, and any 10 of the 14 can rebuild the stripe.

hook: Surviving a region loss usually means a full second copy. How did f4 do it for half the extra cost?
title: f4's XOR trick: survive a region loss at 2.1×, not 2.8×
body:
To survive losing a region, f4 skipped the full second copy. It pairs two volumes in two different regions and stores their **XOR** in a third. Lose any one region and its volume is rebuilt from its **buddy** and the XOR.

Two full encoded copies would cost 1.4 × 2 = 2.8×. With XOR geo-replication it is (1.4 × 2 + 1.4) / 2 = 2.1× per logical byte.

stat.label: effective replication, surviving a region loss

takeaway: One parity volume can stand in for a whole second copy.
deeper:
**Why XOR works:** Store A XOR B separately. If A is lost, A = B XOR (A XOR B), and the same for B. Across regions, it acts as an erasure code with two data pieces and one parity piece.

**The accounting:**
1. Volume A in region A: 1.4× from RS(10,4).
2. Buddy volume B in region B: 1.4×.
3. XOR volume in region C, same size, also 1.4×.
That is 4.2 units of raw disk for 2 logical volumes, so 2.1× per logical byte, against 2.8× for two full copies and 3.6× for Haystack.

**The catch:** Rebuilding after a region loss means reading both the buddy and the XOR from other regions, heavy on cross-region bandwidth. For warm, rarely read data, that rare cost buys a large permanent saving.

quiz.q: Region B is lost. Walk through how f4 recovers a volume that lived there, and what that recovery costs.
quiz.a: Read its buddy volume from region A and the XOR volume from region C, then XOR them to rebuild it. The cost is heavy cross-region reads, acceptable because it's rare.

mcq.q: Where does f4's 2.1× figure come from?
options: Two volumes plus one XOR volume, each 1.4×, shared by 2 volumes
Two full encoded copies at 1.4× each, minus compression
Three replicas stored at 0.7× each using RAID-6
One copy at 1.4× plus a second copy kept on tape
mcq.why: Raw disk is 1.4 + 1.4 + 1.4 = 4.2 for two logical volumes, which is 2.1× per logical byte.

predict.q: f4 survives losing a whole region. What effective replication factor does that cost?

hook: f4 didn't invent a new code. So what earned it roughly 97 petabytes of saved disk?
title: Measure access by age: f4 saved about 97 PB of disk
body:
Back-of-envelope: at 65 PB of logical data, going from Haystack's 3.6× to f4's 2.1× saves 65 × 1.5, about 97 PB of raw disk. That is the kind of number that pays for a whole storage team.

f4 did not win with a clever code. It won by **measuring access by age** and building a cheaper tier for the **long tail**. Before you design a storage tier, get the request-rate-by-object-age curve for your data.
takeaway: The measurement was the innovation; the code was the easy part.
deeper:
**Where leverage came from:** The value wasn't in the coding math. It was the measurement that most BLOBs cool sharply within days or weeks, plus the decision to act on it with a separate system tuned for cold bytes.

**Why it scales so hard:** The saving grows with data size. At 65 PB logical, 1.5× per byte becomes about 97 PB of disks, plus the servers, power, space and operations behind them.

**Reading your own curve:**
1. Steep drop after a week: tiering can save a lot.
2. Flat or unpredictable access: a warm tier may cost more in retrieval and complexity than it saves.

**Same curve, other tools:** It also sets S3 lifecycle rules, like moving photos older than 90 days to a cheaper class while keeping profile photos hot, the same exception Meta made.

quiz.q: Using the f4 math, estimate the raw disk saved if a company with 20 PB of logical data moved from 3.6× to 2.1× effective replication.
quiz.a: 20 × 1.5 = about 30 PB of raw disk saved, because each logical byte drops from 3.6 to 2.1 raw bytes.

mcq.q: Why did f4 succeed, in the senior staff reading?
options: It measured access by age and built a cheap tier for the long tail
It invented a new erasure code with lower overhead
It moved all photos onto faster flash storage
It deleted rarely viewed photos after three months
mcq.why: The coding wasn't the breakthrough; the request-rate-by-age measurement justified a cheaper warm tier for rarely read data.

hook: Meta's hot-photo system ran out of IOPS while its warm system ran out of space. Why was that a design bug?
title: Tectonic: one exabyte-scale system to stop stranding disks
body:
By 2021, Meta had replaced Haystack, f4 and data-warehouse HDFS with **Tectonic**, an exabyte-scale multitenant filesystem (FAST 2021). The reason: specialized systems **strand resources**. Haystack ran out of IOPS with spare capacity. f4 ran out of capacity with spare IOPS. One shared system can use both.

Tectonic scales a single cluster to exabytes, one per datacenter, serving about ten tenants, such as blob storage and the data warehouse.

stat.label: fewer warehouse clusters after HDFS moved over

takeaway: Two half-used systems cost more than one fully used one.
deeper:
**How stranding happens:** Each specialized system is sized for its own bottleneck, so its other resource is left over and can't be lent out. Hot storage needs I/O and has room to spare; warm storage needs space and has idle I/O. On the same drives, the hot tenant uses the I/O and the cold tenant the capacity.

**Metadata that scales:** Tectonic splits metadata into independently scalable layers, Name, File and Block, stored in ZippyDB. Hash partitioning avoids metadata hotspots, the problem S3 users manage with key design.

**Per-tenant choices:** Each tenant picks its own encoding, for example RS(9,6) for long-lived data, so consolidation doesn't force one trade-off on everyone.

**The result:** Moving the data warehouse from HDFS to Tectonic cut the number of warehouse clusters by 10×.

quiz.q: Why does Tectonic hash-partition its metadata instead of partitioning by key range the way S3's index does?
quiz.a: Hash partitioning spreads metadata load evenly and avoids hotspots. Range partitioning can concentrate sequential names on one partition, which S3 users must counter with key design.

mcq.q: Which resource did each of Meta's specialized systems strand?
options: Haystack stranded capacity; f4 stranded IOPS
Haystack stranded IOPS; f4 stranded capacity
Both stranded network bandwidth
Both stranded metadata memory
mcq.why: Haystack ran out of IOPS, leaving capacity unused; f4 ran out of capacity, leaving IOPS unused. Tectonic pools both.

hook: Meta built a specialized photo store, then another, then retired both. Was that a mistake?
title: Specialize, specialize again, then merge: Meta's decade
body:
Meta's photo storage follows a clear arc. **Haystack** specialized for performance, cutting disk operations per read to at most one. **f4** specialized again for cost, moving cooled data to an erasure-coded warm tier at 2.1× instead of 3.6×. **Tectonic** then consolidated everything, including the data warehouse, into one multitenant filesystem.

Each step fixed the previous design's biggest weakness: first I/O, then storage cost, then stranded resources and operations overhead.
takeaway: Every design is right for one stage of growth. None is final.
deeper:
**Stage one, one workload dominates:** A system tuned to its bottleneck wins big. Each usable terabyte in Haystack served about 4× more reads per second than on NAS.

**Stage two, cost dominates:** As data piles up and cools, a second specialized tier pays off. f4 saved roughly 97 PB of raw disk.

**Stage three, overhead dominates:** Several specialized systems each strand a resource and each need their own operations, tooling and capacity planning. Eventually one general multitenant system with per-tenant choices wins. Tectonic kept specialization's benefits through per-tenant encodings, such as RS(9,6) for long-lived data, while pooling I/O and capacity.

**The template:** Optimize for I/O, then for cost with age-based tiers, then consolidate to stop stranding resources. And don't assume today's design is the last one.

quiz.q: A startup with one product and 50 TB of hot data asks whether to build a Tectonic-style multitenant filesystem now. Using Meta's arc, what do you tell them?
quiz.a: Not yet. Consolidation paid off once Meta ran several large specialized systems that stranded resources. With one workload, the right stage is tuning for its bottleneck.

mcq.q: What main weakness did each Meta step fix, in order?
options: I/O, then storage cost, then stranded resources
Storage cost, then I/O, then consistency
Consistency, then I/O, then storage cost
Stranded resources, then I/O, then storage cost
mcq.why: Haystack cut read I/O, f4 cut cost for cooled data, and Tectonic consolidated systems that stranded IOPS or capacity.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
hook: Dropbox moved over 500 PB off Amazon S3. Why would copying that move be a bad idea for most companies?
title: Dropbox left S3: over 500 PB moved to Magic Pocket
body:
Dropbox originally stored file blocks on S3. The **Magic Pocket** project began in 2013, and by October 2015 Dropbox served over 90% of user data from its own infrastructure, after moving over 500 PB. The reasons: end-to-end performance control and better unit economics at its scale.

It worked because the workload is simple (immutable blocks), huge and predictable. For a company with small or spiky needs, it would be a poor decision.

stat.label: moved off S3 into Magic Pocket by Oct 2015

takeaway: Leave the cloud only when your workload is simple, huge and predictable.
deeper:
**Not a config change:** Moving over 500 PB is a multi-year engineering effort. It only makes sense when the benefits are large and lasting.

**What Dropbox bought:** Control over performance means tuning the whole path, hardware, network and software, for one workload instead of the average S3 customer. Better unit economics means that at hundreds of petabytes, owning the storage beats renting it, even after paying a storage team.

**What smaller companies lose:**
1. The decorrelation benefit: in S3, millions of workloads with unaligned peaks share one fleet.
2. A storage team's worth of work S3 does for you: durability, repair, hardware lifecycle.

**The classic case:** Dropbox is the textbook 'leave the cloud' story, and a textbook warning about copying it without its scale.

quiz.q: A 200-person SaaS company with 800 TB of bursty storage cites Dropbox as a reason to leave S3. Give two reasons the comparison fails.
quiz.a: Their workload is small and spiky, so they'd lose S3's decorrelation benefit and pay for their own peaks. They'd also have to staff a storage team, without Dropbox's scale to justify it.

mcq.q: What two reasons did Dropbox give for building Magic Pocket?
options: End-to-end performance control and better unit economics
Stronger consistency and lower request latency
Data residency rules and encryption control
Faster listing and native table support
mcq.why: Dropbox cited control over performance end to end and better unit economics at its scale, after moving over 500 PB.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
hook: Dropbox runs 50 PB storage cells without Paxos-style consensus. What coordinates them instead?
title: Magic Pocket: 4 MB blocks, 1 GB buckets, 50 PB cells
body:
Dropbox's 2016 description of Magic Pocket: files are cut into **blocks** of up to 4 MB. Blocks are grouped into 1 GB buckets, stored in volumes that are replicated or erasure coded across storage machines. A **cell** holds about 50 PB raw.

Each block lives in at least two geographic zones, replicated within about one second. New data is replicated first, erasure coded later. And each cell runs a simple central Master, not a Paxos-based coordinator.
takeaway: Choose the simplest coordinator that works. Consensus is a cost, not a trophy.
deeper:
**Pack small into big:** Tracking billions of 4 MB blocks individually would multiply metadata. Grouping them into 1 GB buckets gives storage machines a manageable number of large units, the same move as Haystack's needles in 100 GB volumes.

**Replicate first, encode later:** Fresh data is replicated for simple, fast handling, then converted to a cheaper erasure-coded form once it settles. Same pattern as Azure's sealed extents and Meta's Haystack-to-f4 path.

**Two zones, one second:** Storing each block in at least two geographic zones, replicated within about one second, protects against losing a site while keeping single-zone exposure short.

**Simplicity on purpose:** Paxos is the consensus approach many systems use for fault-tolerant coordination. Dropbox chose a simple central Master per cell instead, choosing simplicity wherever it could.

quiz.q: Why does Magic Pocket group 4 MB blocks into 1 GB buckets instead of managing each block directly on storage machines?
quiz.a: Fewer, larger units mean far less metadata and bookkeeping per machine. Replication and erasure coding then work on big volumes, the same packing idea as Haystack's needles in large files.

mcq.q: How is each Magic Pocket cell coordinated?
options: By a simple central Master
By a Paxos-based coordinator
By clients computing placement with CRUSH
By a Spanner database shared across cells
mcq.why: Dropbox chose simplicity where it could: each cell has a simple central Master instead of a Paxos-based coordinator.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
hook: Dropbox filled racks with drives that can't rewrite a small region in place. Why was that a smart buy?
title: SMR drives: bad for filesystems, perfect for Magic Pocket
body:
In 2018 Dropbox deployed **SMR** (shingled magnetic recording) drives at petabyte scale. SMR packs tracks like roof shingles, each overlapping the next, so you cannot rewrite a small region in place.

That is a bad fit for most filesystems, which make many small in-place updates. It is a perfect fit for Magic Pocket, whose **extents are append-only and immutable**. With 14 TB SMR drives, one chassis reached about 1.4 PB.
takeaway: Immutability isn't just a software convenience. It lets you buy cheaper hardware.
deeper:
**How the shingle analogy maps:** Roof shingles overlap, so you can't replace one in the middle without lifting the ones on top. SMR tracks overlap the same way, so rewriting one small region means rewriting a larger area around it.

**Old decisions, new options:** Magic Pocket was built around immutable blocks and append-only extents. It never rewrites small regions, so SMR's main drawback simply doesn't apply. A general filesystem constantly updates metadata and file contents in place, which on SMR means rewriting large zones for each small change.

**The payoff is density:** More data per drive means lower cost per byte. One chassis of 14 TB drives reached about 1.4 PB.

**The heat catch:** Denser drives make I/O per terabyte scarcer still. They suit data that is written once and never rewritten, like Magic Pocket's blocks.

quiz.q: A team wants SMR drives under a PostgreSQL cluster to cut cost per terabyte. What's the problem, and what workload would suit those drives instead?
quiz.a: Databases make many small in-place updates, which SMR can't do without rewriting large areas. Append-only, immutable data, like object store extents, suits SMR.

mcq.q: Why can't SMR drives rewrite a small region in place?
options: Their tracks overlap like shingles, so neighbors would be disturbed
Their firmware only accepts writes in 1 GB units
Their platters spin too slowly for random writes
They store parity that must be recomputed per write
mcq.why: Shingled tracks overlap. Rewriting one small region disturbs adjacent tracks, so SMR suits large append-only writes of immutable data.

section: 3.5 Dropbox Magic Pocket and Backblaze Vaults
hook: Backblaze stores your data at just 1.18× overhead. What is it deliberately not protecting against?
title: Backblaze Vaults: 17+3 across 20 pods, 1.18× overhead
body:
A **Backblaze Vault** is 20 Storage Pods. Each file is split into 17 data shards plus 3 parity shards, one shard per pod. Drives in the same position across the 20 pods form a **tome**, and a file lives in one tome.

A Vault survives up to three drive losses in a tome, or three pods offline. Overhead is 20 / 17 = 1.18×. With 20 TB drives, one Vault is about 20.2 PB. Each vault runs in a single site.
takeaway: Low overhead is a choice about which disasters you won't survive.
deeper:
**Three choices behind 1.18×:**
1. Wide stripes: 17 data shards for only 3 parity keeps the parity fraction small.
2. Single site per vault: no multi-zone spread, so no extra parity to survive a zone loss.
3. Cheap commodity pods instead of specialized hardware.

**Compare the neighbors:** Meta's f4 runs 1.4× per cell. The illustrative S3-style scheme that survives a zone loss needed 1.5×.

**Why tomes are clean:** A file's 20 shards sit in the same drive slot across 20 pods, so each pod holds exactly one shard. Any three pods can be offline for maintenance or failure without losing data.

**The trade-off:** A disaster at the site affects the whole vault. And wide stripes mean rebuilding one lost shard requires reading from many pods.

quiz.q: Two pods in a Backblaze Vault are down for maintenance when a drive fails in a third pod. Is any file at risk of loss?
quiz.a: Not yet. A tome survives three lost shards, and two pods plus one drive is three. One more failure in the same tome before repair would lose data.

mcq.q: What is a tome in a Backblaze Vault?
options: Drives in the same position across all 20 pods
The 20 Storage Pods that make up one Vault
The 3 parity shards of a single file
One site holding several Vaults
mcq.why: A tome is the set of same-slot drives across the 20 pods. Each file lives in one tome, one shard per pod.

predict.q: Backblaze splits each file into 17 data + 3 parity shards across 20 pods. What's the storage overhead?
options: About 1.18×
About 1.5×
About 3×

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
hook: MinIO demands one extra healthy drive for writes, but only in one specific setup. Why that setup?
title: MinIO: erasure sets, quorums, and no metadata database
body:
**MinIO** is an S3-compatible object server. Drives form **erasure sets**, 2 to 16 drives by default, and each object is Reed-Solomon coded across one set. With 16 drives, default parity EC:4 gives 75% usable capacity and survives 4 drive failures.

Reads need K healthy drives. Writes need K, or K+1 when parity is exactly half the set, to avoid split-brain. And there is no separate metadata database: metadata travels with each object on the drives.
takeaway: No index means nothing to scale, and nothing to answer 'what's here?' quickly.
deeper:
**What K means:** K is the number of data shards. With 16 drives and EC:4, K is 12, so 12 of 16 drives must be healthy to read.

**Why K+1 at half parity:** When parity is exactly half the set, the set could split into two equal halves, each with exactly K drives, and each could accept conflicting writes. Requiring K+1 guarantees any two write quorums overlap, so split-brain can't happen.

**No metadata database:** Object metadata is stored with the object on the same drives. There is no index service to scale, back up or keep consistent with the data.

**The catch:** Listing and metadata-heavy operations must gather information from the drives themselves. They cost more than in systems with a dedicated index, like S3's sharded index layer or Ceph's bucket index.

quiz.q: An 8-drive MinIO erasure set uses 4 parity. A network split cuts it into two groups of 4. With a write quorum of K, what could go wrong, and how does MinIO prevent it?
quiz.a: K is 4, so both halves could accept conflicting writes: split-brain. Because parity is exactly half the set, MinIO requires K+1 = 5 drives for writes, so at most one side can write.

mcq.q: With 16 drives and default EC:4 parity, what does MinIO give you?
options: 75% usable capacity, tolerating 4 drive failures
80% usable capacity, tolerating 4 drive failures
75% usable capacity, tolerating 2 drive failures
50% usable capacity, tolerating 8 drive failures
mcq.why: 12 data + 4 parity across 16 drives: 12/16 = 75% usable, and any 4 drives can fail.

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
hook: Writes to a big Ceph RGW bucket keep slowing down, yet the cluster looks healthy. What's the usual suspect?
title: Ceph RGW: S3 on RADOS, and the bucket-index trap
body:
Ceph's **RADOS Gateway** (RGW) exposes S3 and Swift APIs on top of RADOS, Ceph's distributed object layer. Objects are placed with the CRUSH algorithm. Bucket listings rely on a **bucket index** stored in RADOS objects.

For big buckets that index must be sharded, and Ceph supports dynamic resharding. Unsharded or under-sharded bucket indexes are a well-known cause of slow writes on large RGW buckets. Multisite configuration replicates between clusters.
takeaway: If every write touches one object, that object is your ceiling.
deeper:
**Metadata over data, open-source edition:** RADOS stores the bytes. A separate bucket index tracks which objects exist in each bucket so listings work. The index itself lives in RADOS objects.

**Why it slows down:** Every write to a bucket updates its index. If one index object covers a huge bucket, every write funnels through it, and write performance drops as the bucket grows. Sharding spreads the index over many RADOS objects so updates proceed in parallel. Dynamic resharding splits it as the bucket grows, similar in spirit to S3 splitting index partitions under load.

**The ops rule:** When a large RGW bucket suddenly slows on writes, check bucket index sharding first.

**What CRUSH adds:** Clients compute where objects live rather than asking a central table, which removes a lookup service from the data path.

quiz.q: An RGW bucket grows from 1 million to 500 million objects on a single index shard, and write latency climbs steadily. Explain the cause and the fix.
quiz.a: Every write updates the one bucket index object, which becomes a hotspot as the bucket grows. Shard the index, or let dynamic resharding split it, so updates spread over many RADOS objects.

mcq.q: Where does Ceph RGW keep the bucket index that listings rely on?
options: In RADOS objects
In a separate PostgreSQL database
Inside each object's own metadata
In the CRUSH map
mcq.why: RGW stores its bucket index in RADOS objects; large buckets need that index sharded to avoid write hotspots.

section: 3.6 Open source: MinIO and Ceph RGW
hook: A storage box passes every S3 API call you throw at it. Can it still silently corrupt your tables?
title: 'S3-compatible' means same API, not same guarantees
body:
A common mistake: assuming 'S3-compatible' means 'behaves like S3'. Compatibility usually means the same API calls work. The **guarantees** behind them can differ.

Consistency on overwrite and list, request-rate scaling, listing performance on huge buckets, and support for newer APIs such as conditional writes and checksums all vary between implementations. The only safe approach is to **test your real workload** on the system you plan to use.
takeaway: An API is a shape. Guarantees are what you're actually buying.
deeper:
**Each gap is hard work:**
1. Consistency: S3 took 14 years and a verified coherence protocol to be strongly consistent for GET, PUT, LIST and DELETE. Another system may accept the same calls and return stale reads after an overwrite.
2. Request scaling: S3 splits index partitions per prefix. Another system may have a fixed limit or a single hot index, like an under-sharded RGW bucket index.
3. Listing: MinIO keeps metadata with objects, so listing costs more than with a dedicated index.

**The silent failure:** Table formats rely on conditional writes for atomic create-if-absent commits. If a compatible system ignored an `If-None-Match` header, two writers could both 'succeed', and a commit would be overwritten with no error.

**Test what you depend on:** Concurrency and failure cases, not just whether uploads and downloads work.

quiz.q: You're moving an Iceberg lakehouse from S3 to an on-prem S3-compatible store. Uploads and downloads pass testing. Name two behaviors you must still test before cutover.
quiz.a: Conditional writes: does If-None-Match really fail with 412 on a race? And consistency of overwrite and list. Listing speed and request-rate scaling on huge buckets also matter.

mcq.q: What does 'S3-compatible' usually guarantee?
options: The same API calls work
The same consistency guarantees as S3
The same per-prefix request rates as S3
Support for every newer S3 API
mcq.why: Compatibility usually means the API calls work. Consistency, scaling, listing performance and newer API support all vary, so test your workload.

hook: One design stores 3.6 bytes per byte of data; another stores 1.18. Which levers explain the gap?
title: From 3.6× replicas to 1.18× stripes: protection compared
body:
Line up the systems. S3: Reed-Solomon across 3 or more AZs, designed for 11 nines. Azure: sync replicas in a stamp, erasure coding of sealed extents, async geo copies. Meta Haystack: 3 replicas plus RAID-6, 3.6×. f4: RS(10,4) plus XOR across regions, 2.1×. Tectonic: per-tenant RS, such as RS(9,6). Backblaze: 17+3 across 20 pods, 1.18×.

Two levers explain most of the gap: **stripe width** and the **size of failure** you insist on surviving.
takeaway: Overhead is the price of the biggest disaster you refuse to lose data to.
deeper:
**The rest of the table:** Google Cloud Storage uses Colossus encodings chosen per application. Dropbox Magic Pocket replicates, then erasure codes, across 2 or more zones. MinIO uses RS per erasure set, such as EC:4. Ceph RGW uses replication or erasure coding in RADOS.

**Lever one, stripe width:** Overhead falls as stripes widen, from Haystack's 3.6× replication to Backblaze's 1.18× wide stripes.

**Lever two, failure size:** A design that must survive losing a whole AZ or region needs more parity or cross-region schemes. A single-site vault can use thin parity.

**Lever three, age:** Several systems change protection as data ages: replicate while hot, erasure code once sealed or cooled, as at Azure, Magic Pocket and Meta's Haystack-to-f4 move.

quiz.q: A team wants Backblaze-level 1.18× overhead but must also survive losing an entire AZ, spreading shards evenly over 3 zones. Why can't they have both?
quiz.a: Surviving a zone loss means parity must cover a third of the shards. With 17+3 over 3 zones, one zone holds about 7 shards, far more than 3 parity, so they'd need much more overhead.

mcq.q: Which system in the comparison has the lowest storage overhead?
options: Backblaze Vault at 1.18×
Meta f4 at 2.1×
Meta Haystack at 3.6×
An f4 RS(10,4) cell at 1.4×
mcq.why: 17 data + 3 parity across 20 pods gives 20/17 = 1.18×, possible because each vault is single-site with wide stripes.

hook: S3, MinIO and Ceph RGW speak the same API. Why is listing a huge bucket cheap on one and costly on another?
title: Where the metadata lives decides what's easy
body:
Same API, different homes for metadata. S3: its own sharded index plus witness cache coherence. GCS: Spanner for permissions and location, Bigtable for Colossus. Azure: a partition layer with range partitions. Haystack: an in-memory needle index per machine. Tectonic: ZippyDB, layered and hash partitioned. Magic Pocket: a per-cell Master plus block index. MinIO: stored with each object. Ceph RGW: a bucket index in RADOS.

The **metadata choice** largely decides what's easy and what's hard in each system.
takeaway: Tell me where your metadata lives and I'll tell you what's slow.
deeper:
**Dedicated partitioned index:** S3, Azure and Tectonic make listing and consistency tractable, but the index must be scaled and kept free of hotspots. S3 partitions by key range; Tectonic hashes to avoid hotspots.

**Globally consistent database:** Keeping metadata in Spanner, as GCS does, makes strong consistency natural.

**Metadata with the object:** MinIO's approach is simplest, with no index to run, but listing and metadata-heavy operations cost more. At the other extreme, an under-sharded index, like an RGW bucket index, becomes a write bottleneck.

**Design ideas, row by row:** S3, massive multitenancy, heat spread, formal checks. GCS, shared Google infra. Azure, stamps and an append-only stream layer. Haystack, one disk I/O per read. f4, a warm tier by age. Tectonic, consolidate all tenants. Magic Pocket, immutable 4 MB blocks on SMR. Backblaze, wide cheap stripes. MinIO, no metadata DB. Ceph RGW, the S3 API on a general object layer.

quiz.q: You need fast listing of a 5-billion-object bucket. Which metadata approach from the comparison fits worst, and why?
quiz.a: Metadata stored with each object, as in MinIO: with no dedicated index, listing must gather metadata from the drives, which is expensive at that scale.

mcq.q: Which system hash-partitions its metadata to avoid hotspots?
options: Meta Tectonic
Amazon S3
Azure (WAS)
Ceph RGW
mcq.why: Tectonic keeps layered metadata in ZippyDB with hash partitioning; S3 and Azure partition by key range, and RGW uses a bucket index.

hook: How can a system built entirely from failing parts make promises as strong as S3's?
title: Immutable data, index-last commits, and checked code
body:
**Immutable objects** in a flat namespace make caching, replication and erasure coding simple, and make in-place updates impossible. Every large object store separates a metadata/index layer from an append-only data layer, and commits a write by writing the **index entry last**.

S3 reached strong consistency in 2020 with a witness acting as a read barrier, backed by proofs and model checking. ShardStore shows lightweight formal methods can be maintained by normal engineers and catch real crash bugs.
takeaway: Freeze the data, commit through the index, and check the code that does both.
deeper:
**Immutability enables the split:** Because data never changes after it's written, the data layer can be simple append-only storage with parity computed once. All the coordination concentrates in the index.

**The commit point:** Data first, index entry last. A crash in between leaves unreferenced garbage, never a visible object with missing bytes.

**Consistency lives there too:** That's why S3's 2020 upgrade focused on keeping its metadata cache coherent. A small in-memory witness tells caches when they're stale, and AWS spent more effort verifying the protocol than building it.

**Same rigor on the node:** ShardStore's executable reference model, about 1% of the code, plus property-based tests with random crashes and disk failures and model checking of concurrency, kept 16 issues out of production.

quiz.q: Connect immutability to S3's commit rule: why does 'data first, index last' work so cleanly for immutable objects?
quiz.a: An object is written once and never patched, so committing it is one step: publish a single index entry after the data is durable. Mutable data would need coordinated partial updates with no single commit point.

mcq.q: Which technique did S3 use to reach strong consistency in 2020?
options: A witness acting as a read barrier for the metadata cache
Removing the metadata cache from the read path
Routing all reads to a single leader per bucket
Adding a delay before any LIST after a PUT
mcq.why: A small in-memory witness lets the cache learn when its view is stale, so S3 kept cache speed and gained strong consistency.

hook: Your storage design review has 30 minutes. Which five questions cover what actually breaks object stores?
title: 11 nines, heat, prefixes, tiers, and moving up the stack
body:
Eleven nines comes from erasure coding across AZs, fast detection and repair, and processes like durability reviews that guard against software and human error. On hard drives the scarce resource is I/O per byte, **heat**, not capacity; wide placement and decorrelation manage it.

S3 scales per prefix: 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second per partitioned prefix, so spread hot keys and retry 503s. Meta's path shows three strategies: I/O, cost, consolidation. And object storage is **moving up the stack**.
takeaway: Ask about repair, heat, keys, age and ownership. Parity is the easy part.
deeper:
**Five design-review questions:**
1. Durability: beyond the coding scheme, how fast is repair, and what guards against bad deploys, GC bugs and operator mistakes?
2. Heat: with about 120 random I/Os per drive regardless of size, how is hot data spread so no drive becomes a tail-latency hotspot?
3. Keys: does the key design spread load, or does a date-first prefix funnel everything into one partition?
4. Tiering: what does the request-rate-by-age curve look like? For f4, it cut effective replication from 3.6× to 2.1×.
5. Ownership: with Express One Zone, Tables and Vectors, will object storage absorb the specialized system you're about to build?

**The pattern behind them:** Hardware failure is the well-understood half. Software, people, physics and cost are where designs actually break.

quiz.q: A new log pipeline writes 15,000 objects per second under keys starting `2026-09-29/`, into a bucket with no versioning. Name the two most urgent problems.
quiz.a: Keys: the date-first prefix funnels all writes into one hot partition, far above 3,500 per second, causing 503s. Durability: without versioning, a bad delete or overwrite is unrecoverable.

mcq.q: On a hard-drive fleet, what is the scarce resource S3 manages as 'heat'?
options: I/O per byte stored
Raw storage capacity
Network bandwidth per region
Metadata memory per index node
mcq.why: Drives hold ever more bytes but still do about 120 random I/Os per second, so I/O per byte, not capacity, runs out.
